Why, evidence and sources

Why it matters

RUBRIC §5 separates adoption from later steps. The Council approved the Convention on 21 Apr 2026, but the EU's ratification took effect with the deposit of its instrument on 15 May 2026. Under Art. 30 entry into force for the EU runs from that deposit date.

Reasoning

Council Decision (EU) 2026/1080 is dated 21 Apr 2026. The Dutch government treaty database lists the EU with "15-05-2026 (R)" (ratification, acceptance or approval), and no other party has ratified.

Uncertainty

The Council of Europe treaty office pages (coe.int) refuse automated access, so the deposit date comes from the Netherlands treaty database, which mirrors the depositary records. Secondary reporting says the deposit was at the 135th Committee of Ministers session in Chisinau.

Carried over, not re-verified

  • Not yet in force: needs five ratifications incl. three CoE member states (the count rule was not re-read in the Convention text this run)

awaiting your decision

Question for you: Should AVERI's context and evaluation note describe its work in its own terms rather than via safety integrity levels and the EU AI Act?

Options

Option a Use AVERI's own framing recommended

avericontext
Now

501(c)(3) launched Jan 15, 2026 by Miles Brundage (formerly OpenAI policy lead). Published an 'AI Assurance Levels' framework on launch — analogous to safety integrity levels in other industries — designed to give regulators and labs a shared scaffold for third-party auditing. Aimed squarely at the bottleneck the EU AI Act exposes: there are far more obligations to verify than independent auditors qualified to verify them.

Proposed

501(c)(3) launched Jan 15, 2026 by Miles Brundage (formerly OpenAI policy lead). Published four 'AI Assurance Levels' on launch — calibrating how much confidence an audit's findings provide — designed to give regulators and labs a shared scaffold for third-party auditing. Names growing the ecosystem of qualified audit providers, rapidly and without compromising quality, as one of the field's most urgent challenges.

avericoverage · eval
Now

Third-party verification capacity for AI assurance — analogous to safety integrity levels in other industries. Aimed at the bottleneck the EU AI Act exposes: more obligations to verify than independent auditors qualified to verify them.

Proposed

Third-party verification capacity for AI assurance — four AI Assurance Levels calibrate how much confidence an audit provides. Aimed at the shortage of qualified independent auditors: AVERI calls for growing the ecosystem of audit providers rapidly without compromising quality.

Cabinet-decided national AI plan under Art. 18 of the AI Promotion Act. First plan Dec 23, 2025; second plan Jul 14, 2026, to be revised in principle annually.

The government's roadmap under the AI Promotion Act, assigning measures to ministries. P-0162 v1 changeVerified externally

EU AI Office: evaluation powers are Art. 92 evaluations and access requests, not pre-deployment access

awaiting your decision

Change

eu-aiocoverage · eval
Now

Can request evaluations from GPAI providers, including pre-deployment access for systemic-risk models. The Scientific Panel of independent experts advises on what to request and how to interpret results.

Proposed

Can evaluate GPAI models itself or through appointed independent experts, requesting access via APIs or source code (Art. 92); the Act gives it no pre-release access, but Code signatories commit to a Safety and Security Model Report, available to the Office by the time a model is placed on the market. The Scientific Panel of independent experts advises on what to request and how to interpret results.

Your response to P-0162 v1
Not answered yet.
Why, evidence and sources

Why it matters

The note tells readers the Office has pre-deployment access to systemic-risk models; the AI Act gives it no such power, which matters for comparing it with AISIs that do test before release.

Reasoning

Art. 92 lets the AI Office conduct evaluations itself or via appointed independent experts and request access through APIs or source code (ai-act p1–p3); nothing in Arts 88–94 gives access before a model is placed on the market (ai-act p8). The Office conducts evaluations rather than 'requesting evaluations from providers'; it can request providers' Art. 53/55 documentation (p7). The closest pre-release element is the GPAI Code: signatories create a Model Report before placing a model on the market and give the Office access by that time (cop-ss p1–p2), with up to 15 business days' delay allowed (p3).

Uncertainty

Implementing acts under Art. 92(6) or later Code practice could add arrangements not yet published.

Carried over, not re-verified

  • The Scientific Panel of independent experts advises on what to request and how to interpret results.

Not answered yet.
Why, evidence and sources

Why it matters

A voluntary evaluator standard became part of how the EU AI Office judges Code compliance for external evaluations, a new link between Layer 4 evaluators and the EU regime.

Reasoning

AEF-1 (v1, 4 Dec 2025) sets operating conditions and a checklist for independent evaluations (aef1 p1–p2, p5). The AI Office's 21 Oct 2026 workshop report says independence of external evaluators under Code Measures 3.2/3.5 should be ensured by contractual safeguards including at least AEF-1's Analytic Autonomy and Transparent Methods sections (ec-evalreq-report p1–p2; ec-evalreq p1). AVERI coauthored it (averi-about p1); METR's Frontier Risk Report used its checklist (aef1 p3). It meets RUBRIC §1 (identifiable text, material via Code compliance, attributable to the Forum, applied by the AI Office); SCOPE B3 admits a standard 'used for regulatory compliance'. Option a recommended because the mechanism is distinct from its authors; b is a lighter alternative.

Uncertainty

The AI Office's view was expressed in bilateral communication and 'may be subject to change' (ec-evalreq-report p3); the Forum is not a legal entity (aef-home p2), so attribution is to a voluntary network.

Why, evidence and sources

Why it matters

The entry tells readers that Australian law gives eSafety AI-specific powers. It does not: eSafety applies general online-safety powers, and AI enters only through instruments it makes under the Act.

Reasoning

The current compilation of the Act (No. 4, 12 Sep 2026) contains no reference to artificial intelligence, generative systems, algorithms or chatbots. Section 145 lets the Commissioner determine industry standards; the 2024 DIS standard, made under s 145, defines a 'high impact generative AI DIS'. So the AI-specific element is the standard, not the Act.

Uncertainty

Absence was established by text search of the compiled Act; uncommenced amendments are not shown in a compilation (the endnotes list none affecting AI). 'World's first online safety regulator' is kept unverified (eSafety's own site was unreachable).

Carried over, not re-verified

P-0002 v2 changeInternal consistency only

FAQ: align 'binding laws' with the map's own classifications (internal consistency only)

accepted v2 · 2026-10-10 · applied 2026-10-10 (2026-10-10-3.json)

Details, evidence and exact wording

Revised from v1: wording changed, so it needs a fresh decision.

Change

index.htmlpage text
Now

Eight binding instruments in this map carry penalty regimes: the EU AI Act (up to €35M or 7% of global revenue), China's GenAI Measures, Korea's AI Basic Act (~$21k per violation), California SB 53 (up to $1M per violation), the Colorado AI Act, the NY RAISE Act ($1M/$3M), Texas TRAIGA, and US BIS export controls. Most are phasing in; several face active federal preemption challenges in the United States.

Proposed

Five AI laws in this map are classed as binding with penalties: the EU AI Act (up to €35M or 7% of global revenue), China's GenAI Measures, Korea's AI Basic Act (~$21k per violation), California SB 53 (up to $1M per violation) and the NY RAISE Act ($1M/$3M). Most are phasing in; several face active federal preemption challenges in the United States. The map's wider count of mechanisms that are binding with penalties also includes US BIS export controls and five regulators: the EU AI Office, UK Ofcom, the UK ICO, Australia's eSafety Commissioner and the Colorado Division of Insurance. The map classes the Colorado AI Act and Texas TRAIGA as hard law with weak enforcement, so they are not counted here.

Why it matters

The FAQ says eight binding instruments and names Colorado and Texas, while the map classes both as pow 3 and its stats tile counts 11 pow-4 mechanisms. Search engines and LLMs ingest this FAQ.

Reasoning

Narrowed from v1. The edit now only aligns the FAQ's list and count with the map's own enforceability classifications and stats tile. It no longer characterises any statute: v1 called Colorado and Texas 'binding statutes' and described the regulators as 'enforcing binding law', both legal claims I had not verified. The penalty figures, 'Most are phasing in' and the preemption sentence are carried over word for word from the current FAQ.

Uncertainty

This is an internal consistency fix. It does not verify the legal status, enforcement or penalties of any law named. Those need the official texts and are queued for the baseline audit. If the baseline finds Colorado or Texas should be pow 4, both the classification and this answer would change.

Carried over, not re-verified

  • Penalty figures (EU €35M/7%, Korea ~$21k, California $1M, New York $1M/$3M)
  • 'Most are phasing in' (consistent with the map's status fields, not externally checked)
  • 'several face active federal preemption challenges'

P-0009 v3 changeVerified externally

New connection NY RAISE ↔ Anthropic RSP: RAISE's framework requirement and Anthropic's separate compliance framework

accepted v3 · 2026-10-10 · applied 2026-10-10 (2026-10-10-2.json)

Question for you: Accept this connection on the RSP entry, or prefer no RAISE↔RSP connection until the map decides how to represent compliance frameworks (for example, noting the FCF in the RSP entry, as P-0010 v3 does)?

Details, evidence and exact wording

Revised from v2: wording changed, so it needs a fresh decision.

Change

ny-raise ↔ rspnew connection
Now

(absent)

Proposed

RAISE requires a published frontier AI framework from Jan 2027; Anthropic says it addresses such requirements with documents including its Frontier Compliance Framework, which is separate from the RSP

Why it matters

The map connects SB 53 and the EU Code to the RSP but not RAISE. Anthropic names all three as framework-publication requirements it addresses. The official texts now settle both open points: what RAISE requires and from when, and how the compliance document relates to the RSP.

Reasoning

Revised from v2 after reading the primary sources. (1) RAISE, as rewritten by Chapter 96 of 2026 (S8828, signed 27 Mar 2026), requires a large frontier developer to 'write, implement, comply with, and clearly and conspicuously publish' a frontier AI framework. It takes effect 1 Jan 2027 (S-0033#2, #3). This RAISE half is now stated in the map's own voice, because the statute was read. (2) Anthropic says SB 53, RAISE and the EU Codes are 'requirements Anthropic addresses through public documentation including its Frontier Compliance Framework' (S-0007#6). The FCF says it 'is distinct from our Responsible Scaling Policy' (S-0010#1). v2 did not say the FCF is a separate document, so a reader would have taken the RSP to be the RAISE compliance route.

Uncertainty

FCF v2 (24 Jul 2026) names only California's TFAIA and the EU Code, not RAISE, which is not yet in effect. So 'addresses such requirements' rests on Anthropic's general statement of Feb 2026, not on a RAISE-specific compliance document. Whether a statute-to-compliance-document link belongs on the RSP entry at all is an editorial choice: the map has no FCF entry, and its existing SB 53 and EU Code connections use the RSP.

P-0010 v3 changeVerified externally

Anthropic RSP: describe the v3 structure (thresholds, ASLs, safeguards, evaluations, timing) and the separate compliance framework

accepted v3 · 2026-10-10 · applied 2026-10-10 (2026-10-10-2.json)

Details, evidence and exact wording

Revised from v2: wording changed, so it needs a fresh decision.

Change

rspcontext
Now

Defines AI Safety Levels (ASLs) — currently up to ASL-3 — each tied to specific capability evaluations and mandatory safeguards: weight-security tiers, deployment mitigations, model-autonomy controls. The original published framework that set the template for the field; commitments include not deploying at a given ASL until the corresponding mitigations are in place. Subjected to detailed external scrutiny in EU GPAI Code drafting and California SB 53.

Proposed

Since v3.0 (Feb 2026) the policy separates Anthropic's own plans from more ambitious industry-wide recommendations, which Anthropic says it cannot commit to follow unilaterally. ASLs now label only the safeguards kept for current models (ASL-3). It adds a Frontier Safety Roadmap of public goals (not hard commitments) and Risk Reports every 3–6 months. The original published framework that set the template for the field. Anthropic's documents for California SB 53 and the EU GPAI Code are a separate Frontier Compliance Framework; the RSP remains its voluntary policy.

rspcoverage · thresh
Now

AI Safety Levels (ASL-1, 2, 3, currently up to ASL-3) trigger graduated safeguards as capabilities cross specified evaluations. The original published framework that set the threshold-and-tier template; SB 53 codifies the underlying norm.

Proposed

Four capability thresholds (non-novel and novel chemical/biological weapons, misaligned AI in high-stakes settings, automated R&D), each mapped to Anthropic's planned mitigations and to recommended industry-wide mitigations. The original published framework that set the threshold-and-tier template; SB 53 codifies the underlying norm.

rspcoverage · eval
Now

Pre-deployment evaluations at each ASL covering CBRN, cyber, autonomous-replication, and AI R&D capabilities. Methodology updated as evaluations mature and external evaluator findings come in.

Proposed

Risk Reports must present capability and alignment evaluations for each threat model, run internally and by external parties as appropriate. Since v3.0 the policy does not pre-specify which evaluations show that a threshold has been crossed.

rspcoverage · timing
Now

Evaluations run pre-training, pre-deployment, and during ongoing operation; thresholds re-checked as capabilities scale. Among the most comprehensive timing regimes in any framework.

Proposed

Risk Reports every 3–6 months cover all publicly deployed models and certain internally deployed ones. Off-cycle risk analyses are due when a significantly more capable model is publicly deployed, and within 30 days of identifying a higher-risk internal model.

rspcoverage · sec
Now

Weight-security tier rises with each ASL — ASL-3 mandates substantially stronger protections against insider threat, exfiltration, and supply-chain attacks. Tied directly to the model's capability profile.

Proposed

Anthropic commits to maintain or improve the ASL-3 security controls it applies to current models, and plans 'moonshot' security R&D for the automated R&D threshold. The security roughly in line with RAND SL4 that it recommends industry-wide at higher thresholds is not a unilateral commitment.

rspcoverage · mit
Now

Deployment safeguards by ASL include refusal training, monitoring, abuse detection, and (at higher ASLs) deployment-environment controls. Specific safeguards published for each tier.

Proposed

Current ASL-3 deployment protections include classifier guards, access controls for trusted users, red-teaming, bug bounties and threat intelligence. For higher thresholds v3 no longer lists required controls; it recommends that developers make a strong argument that risks are contained.

index.htmlpage text
Now

Anthropic (Responsible Scaling Policy, with AI Safety Levels)

Proposed

Anthropic (Responsible Scaling Policy, with capability thresholds and periodic Risk Reports)

Why it matters

The entry describes the pre-v3 policy: an ASL ladder in which crossing capability evaluations triggers specified safeguards for each tier. v3 (Feb 2026, now v3.4) replaced that structure. The ASL wording also feeds the FAQ answer on lab frameworks, which search engines and LLMs ingest. The entry also implies the RSP is what was scrutinised under SB 53 and the EU Code. Anthropic says its compliance document for both is a separate Frontier Compliance Framework.

Reasoning

Each edit is taken from the v3.4 policy text (S-0006); v3.0 (S-0008) already had the same structure. Context: two-tier structure and no unilateral commitment to the industry column (§1, Introduction); ASLs only for present mitigations (Appendix B); Roadmap goals are not hard commitments, and Risk Reports are new (Introduction). The FCF sentence comes from the FCF itself (S-0010#1) and Anthropic's Dec 2025 post (S-0030#1). The RSP also says it handles SB 53-type requirements in separate documents (S-0006#15). Thresholds: the four rows of the §1 table. Evaluations: §3.3 item 3; §1 says evaluations cannot be specified in advance. Timing: §3.1. Security: §1 table, row 1 (ASL-3 controls), the automated R&D row (moonshot security R&D) and the industry column (RAND SL4). Mitigations: §1 table, row 1, and Appendix B. Removed as outdated or unsupported: 'currently up to ASL-3 … each tied to specific capability evaluations and mandatory safeguards'; 'commitments include not deploying at a given ASL until the corresponding mitigations are in place' (pre-v3; v2.0 changelog); 'Subjected to detailed external scrutiny in EU GPAI Code drafting and California SB 53' (not supported by anything inspected, and the compliance document is the FCF); 'autonomous-replication' (replaced by a checkpoint in v2.0, absent from v3); 'pre-training' evaluation timing (absent from v3); 'Specific safeguards published for each tier' (contradicted by Appendix B); and the comparative claim 'Among the most comprehensive timing regimes in any framework' (not checked against other labs).

Uncertainty

The policy text settles what the RSP says. It does not show how Anthropic implements it. The sentences on ASL-3 protections describe commitments, not audited practice. 'The original published framework that set the template' and 'SB 53 codifies the underlying norm' are carried over; Anthropic's own account supports them (S-0007, S-0030), but no independent source was checked. cov.elicit and cov.acct's first sentence are untouched and unverified.

Carried over, not re-verified

  • 'The original published framework that set the template for the field' (context) and '…set the threshold-and-tier template; SB 53 codifies the underlying norm' (thresh): Anthropic's own account only

P-0013 v1 changeVerified externally

Anthropic RSP · Halting: v3 replaced the unconditional pause commitment with competitor-dependent delay commitments

accepted v1 · 2026-10-10 · applied 2026-10-10 (2026-10-10-2.json)

Details, evidence and exact wording

Change

rspcoverage · halt
Now

Anthropic commits to pause development or deployment if mitigations are insufficient for the model's ASL. The halting commitment is the most operationally specific in any lab framework.

Proposed

Since v3.0, Anthropic commits to delay development and deployment in two competitor-dependent scenarios. If it has a significant lead with a highly capable model, it delays until it has a strong argument that catastrophic risk is contained. If all competitors with such models can make that argument, it delays until it matches their risk-reduction posture. Earlier versions committed not to train or deploy models without adequate safeguards, whatever other developers did. Anthropic says it would strongly consider pausing in other cases too.

Why it matters

The map says 'Anthropic commits to pause development or deployment if mitigations are insufficient for the model's ASL' and calls this 'the most operationally specific in any lab framework'. That describes the pre-v3 policy. v3 still has delay commitments, but only in Appendix A's competitor-dependent scenarios. This feeds the halting gap summary, which says every lab framework includes halting conditions.

Reasoning

From v3.4 Appendix A (scenarios and commitments) and its preamble, where v3.1 added 'would strongly consider pausing … even in cases not covered below'. The Introduction says the previous RSP committed to reduce absolute risk 'without regard to whether other frontier AI developers would do the same'. The v2.0 changelog shows the earlier 'commitment not to train or deploy models unless we have implemented adequate safeguards'. v3.0 already had the same Appendix A commitments (S-0008#1), so the change dates from v3.0. The trial-1 caution 'do not infer that pause commitments were removed' holds: they were made conditional, not removed. Also removed: the comparative claim about other labs, which was not checked. 'Highly capable' is the policy's defined term (crossing the automated AI R&D threshold).

Uncertainty

This is the most consequential wording on the entry. It states commitments only; whether any scenario has applied is not evidenced. The policy notes Anthropic often won't know whether a scenario applies and will use its best judgment. The CEO and RSO decide on deployment from each Risk Report, with Board and LTBT approval when marginal-risk arguments are central (§3.4). That is a decision process, not a pause trigger, so it is left out. You may prefer a shorter wording.

P-0014 v1 changeVerified externally

US Frontier AI Access EO: describe EO 14409 from its official text (voluntary cyber-capability access; NSA, Treasury and CISA lead, not CAISI)

accepted v1 · 2026-10-10 · applied 2026-10-10 (2026-10-10-2.json)

Details, evidence and exact wording

Change

us-frontier-access-eolink
Now

https://www.npr.org/2026/06/02/nx-s1-5844347/ai-safety-trump-executive-order

Proposed

https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/06/05/2026-11415/promoting-advanced-artificial-intelligence-innovation-and-security

us-frontier-access-eodesc
Now

EO signed June 2, 2026. Directs federal agencies to establish a framework for voluntary pre-release access (up to 30 days) by frontier-model developers for national-security review.

Proposed

EO 14409, signed June 2, 2026. Directs Treasury, NSA and CISA to design a voluntary framework under which developers may give the government access to 'covered frontier models' (designated by the NSA Director via a classified cyber benchmark) for up to 30 days before release to other trusted partners. Rules out mandatory licensing or preclearance.

us-frontier-access-eocontext
Now

Marks a notable shift in the Trump administration's posture — from deregulation (EO 14179) and state preemption (EO 14365) toward asking for federal access to pre-release frontier models. The 30-day voluntary window mirrors the access agreements UK AISI uses; CAISI is positioned to administer reviews. Whether the framework results in a meaningful national-security review process or remains nominal will depend on developer participation.

Proposed

Marks a notable shift in the Trump administration's posture — from deregulation (EO 14179) and state preemption (EO 14365) toward asking for federal access to pre-release frontier models, though the order itself is scoped to cyber capabilities and rejects 'overly burdensome regulation'. The 30-day voluntary window mirrors the access agreements UK AISI uses. NSA, Treasury and CISA lead; CAISI is not named and NIST is only consulted. Whether the framework results in meaningful federal access will depend on developer participation.

us-frontier-access-eocoverage · eval
Now

Pre-release access (up to 30 days) could enable systematic federal evaluation of frontier models if developers participate.

Proposed

Voluntary early access (up to 30 days) to models the NSA designates through a classified cyber-capability benchmark; scoped to cyber capabilities, not general safety evaluation.

us-frontier-access-eocoverage · timing
Now

30-day pre-release window; voluntary participation.

Proposed

Benchmark and framework due within 60 days of the order; access window up to 30 days before release to other trusted partners; participation voluntary.

us-frontier-access-eocoverage · acct
Now

Federal review mechanism for national-security risks. Departs from prior administration's deregulatory-only posture.

Proposed

Creates no approval or preclearance power (§3(c)) and no enforceable rights (§5(c)). Also directs a Treasury-led AI cybersecurity clearinghouse and a DOJ enforcement priority on AI-enabled computer crime.

Why it matters

The entry's only source is a news article. On the official text, two of its claims are wrong. CAISI does not administer reviews (it is not named; NSA, Treasury and CISA lead, and the NSA Director designates covered models). The order creates no 'review': it sets up voluntary access and expressly rules out preclearance. It also scopes access to cyber capabilities, which the map omits.

Reasoning

All new facts come from the Federal Register text, EO 14409, 91 FR 34565 (S-0038), and its FR API record (S-0039): number, title, signing and publication dates, §3 roles, §3(a) classified cyber benchmark and NSA designation, §3(b) voluntary framework and up-to-30-day access before release to other trusted partners, §3(c) no licensing or preclearance, §2(d) clearinghouse, §4 DOJ priority, §5(c) no enforceable rights. The link moves from NPR to the Federal Register document page, matching the map's other EO entries. The context keeps the map's 'notable shift' analysis and the UK AISI comparison (both carried over), adds that the order itself frames things as reducing regulation (§1), and replaces 'CAISI is positioned to administer reviews'.

Conflicting evidence, resolved (the authoritative (official/legal) text settles it).

NPR (the map's current source) says companies would submit models for the government to 'test up to 30 days before releasing them to the public', and calls this a 'review'. The order says developers may give access 'for a period of up to 30 days before they plan to release such models to other trusted partners'. It does not use the word 'review', and it rules out any preclearance.

The Federal Register text is the legal instrument (91 FR 34565). NPR paraphrases it. Where they differ, on the release reference point and the 'review' framing, the order's own wording governs.

Uncertainty

Whether the benchmark, framework or clearinghouse has been delivered was not checked; no official announcement was found. pow 3 (hard law, weak enforcement) is unchanged. It fits an EO that binds agencies but is voluntary for developers, but that classification is a rubric question for the baseline. The name 'US Frontier AI Access EO' is an informal label and is unchanged.

Carried over, not re-verified

  • 'Marks a notable shift in the Trump administration's posture — from deregulation (EO 14179) and state preemption (EO 14365)': the map's own analysis; the White House frames the order as continuity
  • 'The 30-day voluntary window mirrors the access agreements UK AISI uses': not checked against UK AISI sources

EU AI Act: high-risk application dates moved by the Digital Omnibus (Reg. 2026/1744)

accepted v1 · 2026-10-10 · applied 2026-10-10 (2026-10-10-2.json)

Details, evidence and exact wording

Change

eu-aiadesc
Now

Proposed

In force Aug 2024. GPAI obligations Aug 2025. Most provisions apply Aug 2026; the 2026 Digital Omnibus (Reg. 2026/1744) moved high-risk rules to Dec 2027 (Annex III) and Aug 2028 (Annex I). Penalties up to €35M or 7% global revenue.

Why it matters

The map says high-risk rules apply in Aug 2027. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force since 27 Jul 2026, set 2 Dec 2027 for Annex III systems and 2 Aug 2028 for Annex I systems. Even before that, 'Aug 2027' applied only to Annex I.

Reasoning

The dates come from the Official Journal text of 2026/1744: Art 1(40)(b), replacing AI Act Art 113(c), and Art 4 for entry into force. The Commission's enforcement page agrees. The other clauses were checked and are unchanged. In force Aug 2024 and GPAI obligations Aug 2025 come from AI Act Art 113 (original OJ). Most provisions apply Aug 2026 is the general date, per Omnibus recital 40. €35M/7% is the top penalty tier (Art 99(3)), which the Commission's penalties passage confirms.

Uncertainty

The Omnibus OJ text was read from a copy fetched (HTTP 200) earlier the same day. Later EUR-Lex requests returned empty HTTP 202 responses, and the fetch is recorded as such. The Commission enforcement page (S-0043) independently states the same Annex III and Annex I dates. The Omnibus also brought forward new prohibitions (nudification apps, CSAM) from 2 Dec 2026; these are not added, to keep the edit minimal.

Change

eu-aiacoverage · acct
Now

Why it matters

Both the eu-aia accountability note and the FAQ answer on the AI Office give the AI Office a fine ceiling of €35M or 7%. That ceiling is for prohibited practices. Fines on GPAI model providers, which the Office enforces, are capped at €15M or 3% (Art 101). The FAQ also still says powers 'activate in August 2026', a date that has passed.

Reasoning

From AI Act Art 101(1) (original OJ text, S-0002) and the Commission's enforcement page (S-0043): '€35 million or 7%' for prohibited practices; 'Other breaches, including of the obligations for GPAI models … up to €15 million or 3%'; powers 'apply from 2 August 2026'. The Omnibus (Art 75c(4)) now lets the Office use the Art 99 tiers for AI systems under its new Art 75(1) competence. The highest of those tiers (€35M/7%) is still for prohibited practices only, so 'GPAI providers … €15M / 3%' is the accurate general statement. 'Established January 2024 within DG CNECT' and the Scientific Panel are carried over.

Uncertainty

After the Omnibus, the Office can also fine certain AI systems (those built on a provider's own GPAI model, and those in very large online platforms) under the Art 99 tiers. A fuller description of its new powers belongs to the eu-aio entry, which is outside this trial.

The entry has no source link. It says the law is 'in drafting at NPC' and that 'the 2025 NPC plan dropped it from preparatory items', and its coverage notes describe the contents of 'drafts'. Official sources show there is no published draft. AI legislation is still a preparatory (unscheduled) item in the NPC Standing Committee's 2025 and 2026 plans. It was the State Council's plan that dropped a named 'AI Law draft' in 2025, and its 2026 plan calls for accelerating comprehensive legislation. The 'draft rules on humanlike interactive AI' have since been finalised.

Reasoning

Official texts: NPCSC 2026 and 2025 legislative plans (S-0049, S-0050), §(三) preparatory items. State Council plans for 2026 (S-0051), 2025 (S-0052) and 2024 (S-0053, MOJ copy). The NPC committee's Jan 2026 report on AI-law motions (S-0057) covers MOST-led framework drafting. The NPCSC decision amending the Cybersecurity Law adds Art. 20 on AI, adopted 28 Oct 2025 and in force 1 Jan 2026 (S-0054). CAC Order No. 21 on humanlike interactive AI was issued 10 Apr 2026, in force 15 Jul 2026 (S-0056, S-0055). Removed as unsupported: 'Compute thresholds debated', 'competing proposals from MOST and CAIC' (no official source; 'CAIC' is unidentified), the draft-content claims in the coverage notes (no official draft exists), and 'near-term action looks unlikely' (the State Council's 2026 wording is 'accelerate'). The link is the NPCSC 2026 plan PDF, which settles the NPC status. 'Could consolidate…' softens a speculative claim. status 'proposed' and pow 2 are unchanged.

Uncertainty

None of the plans says whether the eventual instrument will be an NPC law or a State Council regulation. Layer 2 and 'proposed' fit either. The MOJ copy of the 2024 State Council plan and the provincial repost of CAC Order 21 were read from copies a research subagent saved. Later direct fetches got connection resets from those sites, and each source record says so. The NPC draft-consultation database (no AI-law draft through 28 Aug 2026) was checked only by the subagent, so 'No draft has been submitted' rests mainly on the 2026 plan listing AI only as a preparatory item.

P-0020 v1 additionVerified externally

New entry: EU Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-generated Content (Article 50 marking and labelling)

accepted v1 · 2026-10-10 · applied 2026-10-10 (2026-10-10-3.json)

Question for you: Accept as drafted? Optional extras not included, to keep it minimal: (a) a connection to gpai-cop ('Sibling AI Office code; Meta signed this one but not the GPAI Code'); (b) connections to the lab framework entries of signatories (rsp, prep, meta-faif). Say if you want either.

Details, evidence and exact wording

Change

eu-genai-codenew entry · Layer 5 · eu · pow 2 · active

EU AI-generated content code

https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/code-practice-ai-generated-content

Voluntary code (final Jun 2026) for the AI Act's Article 50 duties to mark and label AI-generated content; the Commission and AI Board found it adequate in Jul 2026. Anthropic, Google, Meta, Microsoft and OpenAI signed the provider section.

Two sections: providers commit to machine-readable marking (digitally signed metadata plus imperceptible watermarks) and free detection tools; deployers commit to labelling deepfakes and AI-generated text on matters of public interest. Drafted by independent experts under the AI Office, like the GPAI Code, it gives signatories a recognised route to show compliance with duties that apply from Aug 2026; others must show adequate alternatives to national market-surveillance authorities. Unlike the GPAI Code, Meta signed it.

timing
The underlying Article 50 duties apply from 2 Aug 2026; generative systems already on the market before then have until 2 Dec 2026 for machine-readable marking.
mit
Providers mark outputs with signed metadata and imperceptible watermarks so they are detectable as AI-generated; deployers label deepfakes and AI-generated text published on matters of public interest. Aimed at deception and misinformation, not catastrophic risk.
acct
Signatories must offer detection tools free of charge to users, authorities, researchers and media. Adherence is not conclusive proof of compliance; non-signatories must demonstrate adequate alternatives to market-surveillance authorities.
eu-genai-code ↔ eu-aianew connection
Now

(absent)

Proposed

Code implements the AI Act's Article 50 marking and labelling duties

eu-aio ↔ eu-genai-codenew connection
Now

(absent)

Proposed

AI Office facilitated the drafting by independent experts

Why it matters

A second AI Act code of practice, adopted in July 2026, that the map does not cover. It shapes how every major generative AI provider, including the frontier labs on the map, marks and enables detection of model outputs in the EU. The maintainer asked for it to be drafted (2026-10-10).

Reasoning

Meets RUBRIC §1. It is identifiable (published code text, S-0060). It is material: contextual under SCOPE §C, because it governs deployment-stage marking by GPAI and generative AI providers rather than catastrophic risk. It is attributable: drawn up under the AI Office and assessed as adequate by the Commission and AI Board (S-0046). Layer 5, jur eu, pow 2 and status active mirror gpai-cop, the map's other AI Office code. pow 2 follows RUBRIC §4 ('voluntary government codes'). Every fact comes from Commission pages or the code itself: final publication 10 Jun 2026 (S-0059); adequacy 8 and 9 Jul 2026, and adherence not conclusive proof (S-0046); two sections and non-signatories assessed by market surveillance (S-0045); signed metadata and watermarking (S-0060, Measure 1.1); free detection solution for users, authorities, researchers and media (S-0060, Measure 2.1). Application dates come from the AI Act as amended (S-0041, Art 111(4); S-0045). Section 1 signatories are named by the Commission (S-0058). Meta's absence from the GPAI Code list is from S-0003. Coverage notes are limited to the three METR elements the code actually addresses.

Uncertainty

Signatories can join or leave; the Commission's list is updated continuously (95 Section 1 and 192 Section 2 signatories as of the 31 Jul 2026 page). xAI does not appear. pow 2 versus pow 1 follows the gpai-cop precedent; the rubric's open question on voluntary government codes applies equally. Google is listed as 'Google', and the map's DeepMind framework entry (fsf) is not connected, since the Google signatory may be the company rather than DeepMind.

Seoul commitments: signatories span North America, Europe, Asia and the Middle East, not the UK

Details, evidence and exact wording

Change

seoul-commitcontext
Now

First time a globally diverse set of frontier firms (US, UK, China, UAE, Korea) publicly committed to publishing capability thresholds and the actions they would take if those thresholds were crossed. Voluntary, with no enforcement. But the resulting public pressure created the norm that California SB 53 and NY RAISE later codified into law.

Proposed

First time a globally diverse set of frontier firms (North America, Europe, Asia and the Middle East, including China and the UAE) publicly committed to publishing capability thresholds and the actions they would take if those thresholds were crossed. Voluntary, with no enforcement. But the resulting public pressure created the norm that California SB 53 and NY RAISE later codified into law.

Signatories committed not to develop or deploy models at thresholds where mitigations are insufficient — an explicit halting commitment, voluntarily made by 16 frontier firms spanning North America, Europe, Asia and the Middle East.

Why it matters

The map lists the UK among the signatories' home countries. None of the 16 May 2024 signatories is a UK company as named on the list (Google is listed as Google), while Canada (Cohere) and France (Mistral AI) are left out. The UK Government described the group as spanning North America, Asia, Europe and the Middle East.

The UK Government press release title and first paragraph give the regional spread and name the US, China and the Middle East (seoulpr#p1, seoulpr#p2). The signatory list is in seoul#p1. The edit replaces the country list with the government's own regional description.

Uncertainty

Assigning each firm a home country relies on general knowledge (e.g. Cohere is Canadian, Mistral French), not on these sources, so the edit uses the government's wording rather than a corrected country list. The SB 53 / RAISE sentence in context is analytic and carried over.

Carried over, not re-verified

Delhi commitments: two commitments on usage data and multilingual evaluation; no risk obligations; 13 signatories, fewer than Seoul

accepted v2 · 2026-10-10 · applied 2026-10-10 (2026-10-10-4.json)

Details, evidence and exact wording

Revised from v1: wording changed, so it needs a fresh decision.

Change

delhi-commitdesc
Now

New Delhi Frontier AI Impact Commitments (Feb 2026). 13 frontier developers; broader than Seoul.

Proposed

New Delhi Frontier AI Impact Commitments (Feb 2026). 13 signatories, including four India-based developers; commitments on AI-usage data and multilingual evaluation.

delhi-commitcontext
Now

Extends the Seoul template to cover beneficial use cases — energy efficiency, healthcare, public services — alongside risk obligations. Signatory base broader than Seoul (added Indian and global-south firms) but commitments are weaker on concrete capability thresholds. Reflects the Delhi summit's 'impact' rather than 'safety' framing.

Proposed

Unlike Seoul, contains no thresholds or risk-mitigation commitments. Signatories commit to publish, by the next AI Summit, statistics from anonymised usage data to inform policy on jobs and skills, and to evaluate multilingual capabilities with local ecosystems; progress is to be reported through mechanisms such as the Hiroshima AI Process Reporting Framework. Adds India-based developers (including Sarvam AI and BharatGen) not in Seoul. Reflects the Delhi summit's 'impact' rather than 'safety' framing.

delhi-commitcoverage · mit
Now

Inclusive deployment alongside risk obligations — signatories commit to consider beneficial use cases (energy, healthcare, public services) as well as risk mitigation. Reflects the Delhi summit's 'impact' rather than safety framing.

Proposed

(removed)

delhi-commitcoverage · eval
Now

(absent)

Proposed

Signatories commit to evaluate multilingual capabilities on a subset of languages and cultural contexts and to collaborate with local ecosystems on evaluations for under-represented languages. A stretch: about performance across languages, not dangerous capabilities.

delhi-commitcoverage · acct
Now

Public commitments by 13 frontier developers, including Indian and global-south firms not represented in Seoul. Broader signatory base, weaker on concrete capability thresholds than Seoul.

Proposed

Public commitments by 13 signatories, including India-based developers not in Seoul (including Sarvam AI and BharatGen). Signatories commit to publish usage statistics by the next summit and, where practicable, to report progress through the Hiroshima AI Process Reporting Framework. No enforcement.

Why it matters

The entry describes commitments the text does not contain. The two-page text has two commitments: publish usage statistics and strengthen multilingual evaluation. There are no risk obligations and nothing on energy, healthcare or public services. With 13 signatories it is smaller than Seoul (20), not broader.

Reasoning

Text and signee list (as on 23 Feb 2026) from the summit's outcome document (delhi#p1–p6; observation delhi#p7). PIB release of 19 Feb 2026 for the announcement and the Indian firms (pib#p1–p3). Seoul's count from seoul#p1–p2. The mitigation coverage is removed because the text has no mitigation commitment (delhi#p7). Evaluation coverage is added as a marked stretch (delhi#p4–p5). The accountability note now cites the reporting route (delhi#p1, delhi#p3). Revised before review: the official signee list spells two India-based signees 'Gynani.ai' and 'Socket Labs' (S-0069#6), so the entry names only the two whose spelling the list confirms.

Uncertainty

The list spells two names 'Gynani.ai' and 'Socket Labs'; the PIB release spells them Gnani.ai and Soket, which the edit follows. Comparing the two lists: Amazon, Anthropic, Cohere, G42, Google, Meta, Microsoft, Mistral AI and OpenAI are on both; xAI is not on the Delhi list. The 'impact' framing sentence is carried over.

Carried over, not re-verified

P-0030 v1 changeVerified externally

GPAI Code thresholds: signatories define capability-based risk tiers; the 10^25 FLOP presumption sets scope, not tiers

accepted v1 · 2026-10-10 · applied 2026-10-10 (2026-10-10-4.json)

Details, evidence and exact wording

Change

gpai-copcoverage · thresh
Now

The safety/security chapter calls for capability thresholds tied to systemic risks, mirroring the EU AI Act's 10²⁵ FLOPs trigger. Concrete threshold-setting is left to signatory firms.

Proposed

The safety/security chapter requires measurable systemic-risk tiers defined in terms of model capabilities for each identified risk (Measure 4.1). The AI Act's 10²⁵ FLOP presumption decides which models the chapter covers, not where the tiers sit; concrete threshold-setting is left to signatory firms.

Why it matters

The note says the Code's thresholds mirror the AI Act's 10^25 FLOP trigger. They do not. The FLOP figure is the Act's presumption of systemic risk, which decides who is covered. The Code's thresholds are capability-based risk tiers that each signatory defines.

Reasoning

Measure 4.1 (gpaiss#p1): tiers 'defined in terms of model capabilities', measurable, at least one not yet reached. The 10^25 FLOP presumption is Article 51 classification (gpaiqa#p1, gpaiactqa#p1). The Code does not address the classification thresholds (gpaiactqa#p2). The last clause of the current note is kept.

Uncertainty

None material.

Evidence

    Supports: signatory-defined capability tiers

Pre-dates the frontier-AI debate; its frontier-relevant work is the 2023 Guidance for Safe Foundation Model Deployment and a 2026 report tracking 13 organisations' public disclosure of foundation-model impacts. Most influential as a multistakeholder venue for non-technical issues that frontier-only forums (FMF, AISI Network) skip.

Why it matters

The entry says PAI 'hasn't fully repositioned' to frontier AI without mentioning its frontier-model work. That work is the Guidance for Safe Foundation Model Deployment (2023), a framework for model providers, and a 2026 report tracking 13 organisations against it.

Reasoning

The guidance is described on PAI's home page (paihome#p1). The 2026 report covers 13 organisations and builds on the 2023 guidance (paitr#p1).

Uncertainty

Whether this amounts to 'repositioning' is a judgment; the edit replaces the judgment with the facts. 'AI in journalism' guidance was not checked and is carried over.

Carried over, not re-verified

  • context: 'produces guidance on synthetic media disclosure, AI in journalism, AI workforce impacts.' (synthetic media and workforce checked: paihome#p2, paihome#p3)
  • context: 'Most influential as a multistakeholder venue for non-technical issues that frontier-only forums (FMF, AISI Network) skip.'

OpenAI Preparedness: describe v2 (Apr 2025), not the 2023 beta

accepted v1 · 2026-10-10 · applied 2026-10-10 (2026-10-10-4.json)

Details, evidence and exact wording

Change

prepdesc
Now

Preparedness Framework. Tracked categories (cyber, CBRN, autonomy, persuasion). 2025 revisions tightened bio thresholds.

Proposed

Preparedness Framework v2 (Apr 2025). Tracked categories (bio/chem, cyber, AI self-improvement) with High and Critical thresholds; persuasion moved out of the framework.

prepcontext
Now

Tracks four risk categories (cyber, CBRN, autonomy, persuasion) at low/medium/high/critical levels; deployment requires reaching specific thresholds and implementing graduated mitigations. Decisions reviewed by an internal Safety Advisory Group that escalates to the board. The 2025 revisions reframed the persuasion category and lowered the bio-risk threshold after CBRN evaluation findings. May 2026 added a separate Frontier Governance Framework mapping OpenAI's safety practices to California SB 53 and the EU GPAI Code — a companion governance layer alongside the Preparedness Framework.

Proposed

Tracks three categories (biological and chemical, cybersecurity, AI self-improvement) against High and Critical capability thresholds; Research Categories (e.g. long-range autonomy, sandbagging, nuclear and radiological) are studied but not yet tracked. High capability requires safeguards that sufficiently minimise severe risk before deployment; Critical also requires them during development. An internal Safety Advisory Group recommends, OpenAI Leadership decides, and the board's Safety and Security Committee oversees. In September 2026 OpenAI designated GPT-6 Astra its first model at the Critical cybersecurity level. May 2026 added a separate Frontier Governance Framework mapping OpenAI's safety practices to California SB 53 and the EU GPAI Code — a companion governance layer alongside the Preparedness Framework.

prepcoverage · thresh
Now

Tracks four risk categories (cyber, CBRN, autonomy, persuasion) at low/medium/high/critical levels; deployment requires specific thresholds and graduated mitigations. Different threshold structure from Anthropic's ASLs — category × level matrix rather than single-axis tier.

Proposed

Three Tracked Categories (bio/chem, cyber, AI self-improvement), each with High and Critical capability thresholds; v2 dropped the low and medium levels. Different threshold structure from Anthropic's ASLs — category × level matrix rather than single-axis tier.

prepcoverage · eval
Now

Evaluations against tracked categories run pre-deployment and ongoing; methodology disclosed in the framework and updated 2024–2025. External evaluators (METR, Apollo) participate.

Proposed

Automated scalable evaluations on every covered model before deployment, validated by expert-led deep dives; methodology set out in the framework (v2, 2025). External evaluators (METR, Apollo, UK AISI) participate.

prepcoverage · elicit
Now

Capability elicitation through adversarial scaffolding, red-teaming, and agentic deployment is built into the evaluation protocols. Apollo's scheming research has shaped the autonomy category specifically.

Proposed

Evaluations aim to approximate the high end of elicitation by threat actors — highest-capability settings, a model variant with negligible safety refusals, the best available scaffolds, fine-tuning if weights will be released — and treat results as a lower bound. Sandbagging is a Research Category.

prepcoverage · sec
Now

Weight security obligations scale with risk level; high/critical-risk models trigger enhanced protections. Specific tier definitions disclosed in the framework.

Proposed

Security controls meeting a High standard (threat modelling, defence in depth, access management and related practices) are required for High-capability models; the framework says a Critical standard is still to be specified.

prepcoverage · mit
Now

Deployment safeguards graduated by risk level — refusals, monitoring, agentic controls, deployment-environment restrictions. Critical-risk gates production deployment outright.

Proposed

Safeguards against malicious users (refusal training, usage monitoring, trust-based access) and against misaligned models (alignment, oversight, restricted system architecture), documented in Safeguards Reports. High-capability models deploy only once safeguards sufficiently minimise severe risk.

prepcoverage · halt
Now

High and critical risk levels gate deployment; OpenAI commits not to ship at those levels until mitigations reduce risk to medium or below. Explicit halting commitment subject to internal Safety Advisory Group review.

Proposed

Commits not to deploy High-capability models until safeguards sufficiently minimise the associated severe risk, and for Critical capability to halt further development until safeguards and security controls meeting a Critical standard are specified. May adjust safeguards if a rival ships a comparable system without them, but only with public acknowledgement and while staying more protective.

prepcoverage · acct
Now

Internal Safety Advisory Group reviews evaluations and escalates to the board for high/critical-risk decisions. External transparency is through the published framework rather than reporting to a regulator.

Proposed

Safety Advisory Group reviews Capabilities and Safeguards Reports and recommends; OpenAI Leadership makes final decisions, overseen by the board's Safety and Security Committee, which can reverse them. Results are published with system cards; the separate Frontier Governance Framework covers incident reporting to authorities under SB 53 and the EU Code.

prepcoverage · update
Now

Framework updated in 2024 and 2025; the 2025 revision reframed the persuasion category and lowered the bio-risk threshold after CBRN evaluation findings.

Proposed

Beta Dec 2023; v2 Apr 2025 dropped persuasion and the low/medium levels, split model autonomy and added Research Categories. Commits to review the framework at least once a year.

Why it matters

The entry describes the December 2023 beta (four categories including persuasion, low-to-critical scale, "medium or below" deployment rule, board escalation). OpenAI replaced it in April 2025; readers comparing labs get OpenAI's current commitments wrong, including its halting language and governance. Astra (Sep 2026) is the first model OpenAI designated Critical.

Reasoning

Preparedness Framework v2 (still the version OpenAI links from its Sep 2026 Astra post and system card) sets three Tracked Categories, High/Critical thresholds, moves persuasion out, commits to halt further development at Critical until a Critical standard exists, and sets SAG → Leadership → board SSC governance. The beta is the source of the current wording. The "2025 revisions tightened/lowered bio thresholds" claim has no support in v2's change log. Evaluator participation comes from the GPT-5.6 (METR) and GPT-6 Astra (Apollo, UK AISI) system cards.

Uncertainty

v2 has no public successor as of 10 Oct 2026 (checked OpenAI's framework-tagged news list and the Astra post/card); OpenAI said in v2 it expected to update the framework before reaching Critical, so a v3 may follow. The Astra designation is OpenAI's own assessment.

Carried over, not re-verified

  • "Different threshold structure from Anthropic's ASLs — category × level matrix rather than single-axis tier" (comparative; RSP v3 now uses ASLs only for safeguards)
  • FGF sentence in context (checked against the FGF; kept verbatim)

GDM Frontier Safety Framework: correct versions and describe v3.1

accepted v1 · 2026-10-10 · applied 2026-10-10 (2026-10-10-4.json)

Details, evidence and exact wording

Change

fsfdesc
Now

Critical Capability Levels and mitigations. v3 (April 2026) is the current version; v2 (2024) added explicit deceptive-alignment evaluations.

Proposed

Critical Capability Levels and mitigations. v3.1 (17 Apr 2026) is the current version and added lower Tracked Capability Levels; v2 (Feb 2025) added a deceptive-alignment approach.

fsfcontext
Now

Defines Critical Capability Levels (CCLs) across cyber-offence, biorisk, ML R&D, and deceptive-alignment domains; each CCL maps to concrete security and deployment mitigations. v2 (2024) added explicit deceptive-alignment evaluations after Apollo Research findings; subsequent updates extended the autonomous-task evaluation strand. Less prescriptive than Anthropic's RSP on halting commitments — relies more on internal review than published red-lines.

Proposed

Defines Critical Capability Levels (CCLs) in CBRN, cyber, harmful manipulation and ML R&D, with lower Tracked Capability Levels (TCLs) for CBRN and for misalignment (stealth and situational awareness); each CCL carries a recommended security level and a deployment-mitigation process that needs a safety case. v2 (Feb 2025) added a deceptive-alignment approach; v3 (Sep 2025) added harmful manipulation; v3.1 (Apr 2026) folded misalignment into a combined ML R&D and misalignment domain. Less prescriptive than Anthropic's RSP on halting commitments — relies more on internal review than published red-lines.

fsfcoverage · thresh
Now

Critical Capability Levels (CCLs) defined across cyber-offence, biorisk, ML R&D, and deceptive-alignment domains. Capability-tier framing — somewhere between Anthropic's ASLs and OpenAI's category × level matrix.

Proposed

Critical Capability Levels (CCLs) in CBRN, cyber, harmful manipulation and ML R&D, plus lower Tracked Capability Levels (CBRN; stealth and situational awareness) added in v3.1. Capability-tier framing — somewhere between Anthropic's ASLs and OpenAI's category × level matrix.

fsfcoverage · elicit
Now

v2 (2024) added explicit deceptive-alignment evaluations after Apollo Research findings — among the first lab frameworks to formally adopt scheming evaluations as a capability-elicitation strand.

Proposed

Evaluations apply scaffolding, inference compute and other augmentations to assess the systems likely to be built on the model; per-model FSF reports describe agentic scaffolding and sandbagging checks. v2 (Feb 2025) added instrumental-reasoning (deceptive-alignment) levels, now the stealth and situational awareness TCL.

fsfcoverage · timing
Now

Evaluations run periodically rather than at strict pre-training/pre-deployment milestones. Less granular timing structure than Anthropic's RSP.

Proposed

Critical capability assessment before a model's first external deployment; material-capability-change assessments on checkpoints after post-training runs decide whether later versions need a new one. Alert thresholds flag approach to a CCL between assessments.

fsfcoverage · sec
Now

Security mitigations per CCL — protections scale with the capability profile. Specifics published in the framework but less granular than Anthropic's tier system.

Proposed

Recommended security level per CCL, aligned with RAND levels: Security Level 2+ (SL2 plus insider-threat and non-state-actor measures) for CBRN, cyber and harmful manipulation; SL3 and SL4 for the ML R&D CCLs. Framed as the minimum the field should apply.

fsfcoverage · halt
Now

Halts at critical levels are committed pending mitigation review — but the halting trigger is less prescriptive than Anthropic's RSP, relying more on internal review than published red-lines.

Proposed

Commits that external deployments (and, for ML R&D and misalignment levels, high-risk internal deployments) proceed only after a governance function finds residual risk acceptable, with a safety case once a CCL is reached; for misuse levels this applies to external deployment, not further development. Relies more on internal review than published red-lines.

fsfcoverage · update
Now

v2 (2024) added deceptive-alignment evaluations after Apollo Research findings; v3 (April 2026) extended the autonomous-task evaluation strand. Update cadence less formalised than Anthropic's RSP.

Proposed

v1 May 2024; v2 Feb 2025 (security levels, deceptive-alignment approach); v3 Sep 2025 (harmful manipulation, ML R&D protocols); v3.1 Apr 2026 (TCLs, SL2+, governance section). Commits to review at least once a year.

Why it matters

The entry dates v2 to 2024 and calls the April 2026 text "v3"; v3 was September 2025 and April 2026 is v3.1. It lists a biorisk/deceptive-alignment domain set that no longer exists, attributes v2 to Apollo findings with no support, and describes a halting commitment and timing structure that v3.1 does not contain.

Reasoning

FSF v3.1 (17 Apr 2026) lists its version history, its four risk domains, TCLs, security levels, pre-first-deployment assessments, and deployment gates. DeepMind's Feb 2025 post introduces the deceptive-alignment approach without mentioning Apollo. v3.1 contains no "halt", "pause", "on hold" or "stop"; its gates are deployment conditions, written here as commitments.

Uncertainty

The "less prescriptive than Anthropic's RSP" characterisation is carried over and analytic. Whether the Feb 2025 deceptive-alignment approach drew on Apollo research is not shown either way; the text simply drops the claim.

Carried over, not re-verified

  • "Less prescriptive than Anthropic's RSP on halting commitments — relies more on internal review than published red-lines" (analytic)
  • "Capability-tier framing — somewhere between Anthropic's ASLs and OpenAI's category × level matrix" (analytic)

P-0039 v1 changeVerified externally

Meta framework: describe v2 thresholds and the change from "stop" to "develop with mitigations"

accepted v1 · 2026-10-10 · applied 2026-10-10 (2026-10-10-4.json)

Details, evidence and exact wording

Change

meta-faifcontext
Now

Two-tier risk classification: high-risk released with mitigations, critical-risk not released at all until mitigations reduce the risk to high. Explicit commitment not to ship critical-risk models — the headline differentiator with xAI's framework. The only major US lab to refuse the EU GPAI Code, putting Meta's compliance route under the AI Act in question.

Proposed

Risk thresholds (critical, high, moderate or lower) across chemical and biological, cyber and, since v2, loss of control. v2 replaced "stop" at the critical threshold with "develop with mitigations": Meta commits to deploy high- or critical-threshold models only once validated mitigations reduce risk to that of a moderate-or-lower model, and to continue developing a critical-threshold model only if catastrophic risks are within acceptable levels. The only major US lab to refuse the EU GPAI Code, putting Meta's compliance route under the AI Act in question.

meta-faifcoverage · thresh
Now

Two-tier classification — high-risk (released with mitigations) and critical-risk (not released until mitigations reduce risk to high). Coarser than Anthropic's ASLs or OpenAI's category × level matrix.

Proposed

Three thresholds — critical, high, moderate or lower — set by whether a model would substantially contribute to a threat scenario for a catastrophic outcome in chemical and biological, cyber or loss-of-control risk. Coarser than Anthropic's ASLs or OpenAI's category × level matrix.

meta-faifcoverage · eval
Now

Evaluations against the two risk tiers; less methodological detail published than peers. External evaluator participation limited.

Proposed

Risk assessments against the thresholds before release, with a published preparedness report for each closed or open Frontier AI release describing evaluations, methodology and evaluator access. External experts join threat modelling where relevant.

meta-faifcoverage · elicit
Now

Adversarial testing performed pre-deployment; specifics not heavily disclosed. Less developed than the elicitation work in RSP, Preparedness, or FSF.

Proposed

Commits to assess with maximum elicitation in mind — evaluating the model as part of a system with the scaffolding and tooling available for the proposed deployment — to capture the upper bound of risk.

meta-faifcoverage · timing
Now

Pre-deployment evaluation; ongoing monitoring at the tier level. Update cadence and trigger conditions not heavily specified.

Proposed

Assessments during development and before release; a new preparedness report is triggered by a newly pre-trained model, a large compute increase or changes that materially increase relevant capabilities, with preliminary assessments before controlled deployments.

meta-faifcoverage · mit
Now

Deployment mitigations layered onto release — high-risk models ship with mitigations; critical-risk models don't ship at all. Mitigation specifics discretionary.

Proposed

Mitigations required before deployment at the high threshold and before further development at the critical threshold, validated to reduce risk to moderate or lower; specific measures adapt to each scenario.

meta-faifcoverage · halt
Now

Explicit commitment not to ship critical-risk models — the headline differentiator from xAI's framework. Halting trigger tied to the binary tier rather than graduated capabilities.

Proposed

v2 (Apr 2026) changed the critical threshold from "stop" to "develop with mitigations": Meta commits to continue development only if catastrophic risks are within acceptable levels and to deploy only after validated mitigations reduce risk to moderate or lower.

meta-faifcoverage · acct
Now

Internal review; thinner external accountability surface than peers. Refused to sign the EU GPAI Code, putting Meta's compliance route under the AI Act in question.

Proposed

Chief AI Officer oversees the process and approves deployments, supported by a Director of Alignment and Risk; the Board oversees regulatory compliance; preparedness reports are published per release, with whistleblower and non-compliance reporting. Refused to sign the EU GPAI Code, putting Meta's compliance route under the AI Act in question.

meta-faifcoverage · update
Now

Released Feb 2025 after pressure; revision schedule not publicly committed. Among the slowest-evolving lab frameworks.

Proposed

Released Feb 2025; v2 (Apr 2026) renamed it Advanced AI Scaling Framework and revised thresholds, domains and governance. Commits to review at least annually.

Why it matters

The entry still describes "critical-risk not released at all" as Meta's headline commitment. Meta's v2 (7 Apr 2026) explicitly changed the critical measure from "Stop" to "Develop with Mitigations", added loss of control and named accountable officers, so the map overstates Meta's halting commitment and understates its new transparency commitments.

Reasoning

Meta's v2 PDF (linked from the map entry) has a change log recording each change, the three-threshold table, the development and deployment conditions, the governance roles, preparedness-report triggers, maximum-elicitation language and the annual review commitment. The EC signatory list still omits Meta.

Uncertainty

The "only major US lab to refuse" and "coarser than" phrases are carried over and analytic; xAI signed only the Safety and Security Chapter. Even v1 framed critical as stop-development rather than "not released until risk reduced to high", so the current text was inaccurate before v2.

Carried over, not re-verified

  • "The only major US lab to refuse the EU GPAI Code, putting Meta's compliance route under the AI Act in question" (Meta's absence from the list verified; "only" and the consequence are analytic)
  • "Coarser than Anthropic's ASLs or OpenAI's category × level matrix" (analytic)

P-0041 v1 changeVerified externally

xAI framework: current edition (30 Jun 2026), lifecycle timing and acceptance commitment

accepted v1 · 2026-10-10 · applied 2026-10-10 (2026-10-10-4.json)

Details, evidence and exact wording

Change

xai-rmfdesc
Now

Published Feb 2025 after delay. Thinner than peers. xAI suing Colorado over AI Act.

Proposed

Draft Feb 2025; final Risk Management Framework Aug 2025, renamed Frontier AI Framework Dec 2025; current edition effective 30 Jun 2026. Thinner than peers. xAI suing Colorado over AI Act.

xai-rmfcontext
Now

Quantitative-benchmark approach to capability evaluation (chosen benchmarks rather than red-lined capability thresholds), with internal review processes. Independent reviews of frontier risk-management frameworks have flagged the narrow scope of risk tolerances and limited halting commitments as gaps. xAI's litigation against Colorado SB 24-205 makes it the most visible lab opponent of state-level AI regulation in the US.

Proposed

Earlier editions set benchmark-based acceptance criteria (e.g. answering under 1 in 20 restricted bio/chem queries; MASK dishonesty under 1 in 2); the 30 Jun 2026 edition is restructured along the EU GPAI Code's Safety and Security Chapter, covering CBRN, offensive cyber, loss of control and harmful manipulation, and states no numeric criteria. Independent reviews of frontier risk-management frameworks have flagged the narrow scope of risk tolerances and limited halting commitments as gaps. xAI's litigation against Colorado SB 24-205 makes it the most visible lab opponent of state-level AI regulation in the US.

xai-rmfcoverage · thresh
Now

Quantitative-benchmark approach — emphasises specific benchmark scores (e.g., bio/chem answer rates) rather than red-lined capability thresholds. Independent reviews of frontier risk-management frameworks have flagged the narrow scope and absence of well-defined risk tolerances as gaps.

Proposed

Risk acceptance by reviewing systemic-risk tiers per domain (CBRN, offensive cyber, loss of control, harmful manipulation) using public and internal benchmarks; the Jun 2026 edition states no numeric criteria, where earlier editions set benchmark limits such as answering under 1 in 20 restricted bio/chem queries. Independent reviews of frontier risk-management frameworks have flagged the narrow scope and absence of well-defined risk tolerances as gaps.

xai-rmfcoverage · timing
Now

Pre-deployment evaluation only; ongoing monitoring or re-evaluation triggers not heavily specified. Less comprehensive lifecycle coverage than peers.

Proposed

Risk management across the model lifecycle, including post-market monitoring; a full systemic risk assessment at least yearly, with smaller evaluations at triggers such as an updated model, a serious incident or materially increased risk.

xai-rmfcoverage · halt
Now

Limited halting commitments — independent analyses have flagged the absence of clear pause triggers. Distinguishes xAI from Meta's explicit critical-risk halt.

Proposed

Commits to proceed with development, market release or use only if systemic risks are determined acceptable, and may temporarily shut down a system during an incident; defines no capability-specific pause triggers. Independent analyses have flagged the absence of clear pause triggers.

xai-rmfcoverage · update
Now

Framework released after delay (Feb 2025); revision schedule not publicly committed.

Proposed

Draft Feb 2025 promised an update within three months; final RMF Aug 2025, renamed Frontier AI Framework Dec 2025 and revised again Jun 2026 without a published change log. Commits to periodic review.

Why it matters

The entry dates xAI's framework to February 2025 (a draft) and describes only its benchmark-threshold approach. xAI has since issued three editions; the current one (effective 30 Jun 2026) follows the EU Code's Safety and Security Chapter, adds lifecycle and annual-assessment commitments, and drops the numeric criteria. The halt note also compares xAI with a Meta "critical-risk halt" that Meta revised in April 2026.

Reasoning

The four xAI PDFs (Feb 2025 draft, Aug 2025 RMF, Dec 2025 FAIF, Jun 2026 FAIF) and the x.ai/safety page show the sequence and current text; the DOJ press release confirms xAI sued over SB24-205 on 9 Apr 2026.

Uncertainty

"Thinner than peers", the independent-review sentences and "most visible lab opponent" are carried over and not checked. The Dec 2025 edition said it complies with the TFAIA; the Jun 2026 edition does not mention the TFAIA — recorded here, not interpreted. The litigation was reportedly stayed in late April 2026 (secondary sources only).

Carried over, not re-verified

  • "Thinner than peers" (analytic)
  • "Independent reviews of frontier risk-management frameworks have flagged …" sentences (secondary claims, not checked)
  • "most visible lab opponent of state-level AI regulation in the US" (analytic)

NIST confirms the San Diego meeting in Dec 2025.

Uncertainty

The membership list is unchanged and confirmed by sources from Dec 2025 and Jul 2026. 'US/CAISI' and 'France INESIA' name institutes, whereas the sources list countries; NIST and the AISI blog confirm CAISI and INESIA participate.

P-0049 v1 changeVerified externally

OECD AI Principles: adherent count is out of date (50 countries plus the EU, May 2026)

accepted v1 · 2026-10-10 · applied 2026-10-10 (2026-10-10-4.json)

Details, evidence and exact wording

Change

oecddesc
Now

2019, updated 2024. 47 countries.

Proposed

2019, updated 2024. 50 countries plus the EU adhere (May 2026).

Why it matters

The count is wrong twice over. The official register lists 51 adherents (38 OECD members, 12 non-members and the EU), and the current '47' counts the EU as a country.

Reasoning

The OECD Compendium of Legal Instruments is the official register for OECD/LEGAL/0449. It lists four non-member adherents missing from the OECD.AI overview page: Uruguay (1 Oct 2024), Saudi Arabia (5 Jun 2025), Cambodia and Croatia (both 15 May 2026). It also lists the EU separately under 'Other'.

Conflicting evidence, resolved (the authoritative (official/legal) text settles it).

The OECD.AI overview page says there are 47 adherents. The OECD Compendium of Legal Instruments lists 38 Members, 12 Non-Members and the EU (51).

The Compendium is the OECD's official register of adherence to its legal instruments and gives a dated adherence for each non-member. The OECD.AI list omits exactly the four countries that adhered from Oct 2024 onwards (Uruguay, Saudi Arabia, Cambodia, Croatia), so it is a stale summary, not a different definition.

Uncertainty

Counts drift, so the date is included. An alternative is stable phrasing: 'all OECD members plus 12 other countries and the EU'.

P-0050 v1 changeVerified externally

OECD coverage note: transparency/explainability and accountability are two of the five principles, not three

accepted v1 · 2026-10-10 · applied 2026-10-10 (2026-10-10-4.json)

Details, evidence and exact wording

Change

oecdcoverage · acct
Now

Transparency, explainability, and accountability are three of the five values-based principles. Adopting countries are encouraged to embed them in domestic frameworks rather than report on them.

Proposed

Transparency and explainability, and accountability, are two of the five values-based principles. Adopting countries are encouraged to embed them in domestic frameworks rather than report on them.

Why it matters

Simple factual slip. 'Transparency and explainability' is one principle, so with 'Accountability' that makes two of the five.

Reasoning

The Recommendation's five principles are: i) inclusive growth…; ii) rule of law, human rights…; iii) transparency and explainability; iv) robustness, security and safety; v) accountability.

Uncertainty

The second sentence is carried over. The Recommendation instructs the OECD's Digital Policy Committee to report to Council on implementation, so 'rather than report on them' is arguable for the OECD as a whole, though adherents have no individual reporting duty in the text.

Carried over, not re-verified

  • Adopting countries are encouraged to embed them in domestic frameworks rather than report on them.

Change

Proposed

First binding international AI treaty (opened for signature Sept 2024). Signatories include EU, UK, US, Japan; only the EU has ratified (approved Apr 2026). Not yet in force: needs five ratifications incl. three CoE member states.

Why it matters

Readers need to know the treaty is not in force and how far it is from entry into force. The EU's conclusion in 2026 is the only ratification so far.

Reasoning

Council Decision (EU) 2026/1080 of 21 April 2026 approves the Convention on behalf of the EU (OJ 13 May 2026). The CoE convention page lists the EU as the sole Party. EUR-Lex shows the Convention as 'not yet in force'. Article 30(3) requires five signatories, including at least three CoE member states, to consent before entry into force.

Uncertainty

The CoE Treaty Office chart (signatures and ratifications table) could not be rendered: its JavaScript bundle is refused. The Party/signatory lists come from the CoE AI convention page, rendered in headless Chromium today. The exact EU deposit date (reported elsewhere as 15 May 2026) was not seen in a primary source, so the edit uses the Council approval month.

P-0054 v1 additionVerified externally

New entry: UN Independent International Scientific Panel on AI and Global Dialogue on AI Governance

accepted v1 · 2026-10-10 · applied 2026-10-10 (2026-10-10-4.json)

Details, evidence and exact wording

Change

un-ainew entry · Layer 1 · mu · pow 1 · active

UN AI Panel & Dialogue

https://www.un.org/independent-international-scientific-panel-ai/en

UN General Assembly resolution 79/325 (Aug 2025) created a 40-member Independent International Scientific Panel on AI and an annual Global Dialogue on AI Governance. The Panel (co-chairs Yoshua Bengio, Maria Ressa) issued its Preliminary Report in Jul 2026 and a brief on AI agents and loss of control in Sep 2026; the first Dialogue met in Geneva in Jul 2026.

The UN's universal-membership counterpart to the International AI Safety Report and the summit series. The Panel's annual report is policy-relevant but non-prescriptive and is presented at the Dialogue, a platform whose topics include safe, secure and trustworthy AI, human rights and interoperable governance; its outcomes are co-chairs' summaries, not negotiated texts. Non-military domain only. The Sep 2026 brief, on AI agents that breached Hugging Face's systems while under evaluation at OpenAI, put loss-of-control risk on the UN agenda.

eval
Synthesises scientific evidence on AI capabilities, risks and safeguards rather than testing models itself; its first thematic brief assessed a real incident involving AI agents under evaluation.
acct
Annual report presented to governments at the Global Dialogue, plus up to two updates a year to the General Assembly plenary. No enforcement: accountability through shared evidence and public debate.
update
One annual report plus thematic briefs as the Panel deems necessary; the Dialogue meets annually, alternating between Geneva and New York (next: New York, May 2027).
un-ai ↔ aisrnew connection
Now

(absent)

Proposed

AISR positions itself as complementary to the UN Panel; Bengio chairs both

un-ai ↔ unesconew connection
Now

(absent)

Proposed

UNESCO co-coordinates the Global Dialogue's joint secretariat with ITU

ai-summits ↔ un-ainew connection
Now

(absent)

Proposed

Paris summit statement reaffirmed support for launching the Panel and Dialogue

Why it matters

A UN body with an adopted General Assembly mandate that now issues frontier-relevant scientific assessments, including a Sep 2026 brief on AI-agent misalignment and loss of control. The Global Dialogue is the only universal-membership intergovernmental forum on AI governance. SCOPE B3 allows a UN body as a proposed addition when it has an adopted mandate bearing on frontier/GPAI governance.

Reasoning

RUBRIC §1. Identifiable: A/RES/79/325 of 26 Aug 2025. Material: direct bearing, because the Dialogue's mandate includes 'safe, secure and trustworthy' AI and the Panel's outputs address deceptive behaviour and loss of control in advanced AI. Attributable: UNGA established both; the Panel has 40 members, and the Dialogue is convened under GA co-chairs. Layer 1 (intergovernmental report and forum, like aisr and ai-summits); jur mu. pow 1 matches aisr (non-binding synthesis); pow 2 is arguable because it is GA-established. Status active: the Preliminary Report (1 Jul 2026), thematic brief (21 Sep 2026) and first Dialogue (6–7 Jul 2026) have all happened.

Uncertainty

pow 1 vs 2 is a classification judgement. One combined entry is proposed because the resolution creates the two bodies together and the Panel reports to the Dialogue; they could be split. The first comprehensive report is due in 2027.
