P-0055 v1 changeVerified externally

SB 53: transparency reports are per deployment, not annual; 15-day window is not the tightest state window

accepted v1 · 2026-10-10 · applied 2026-10-10 (2026-10-10-4.json)

Details, evidence and exact wording

Change

ca-sb53context
Now

Requires 'large frontier developers' to publish a frontier safety framework, report critical safety incidents within 15 days, and submit annual transparency reports. Whistleblower protections for employees flagging safety issues. The first US state law to codify the published-framework norm — explicitly anchors against Layer 6 lab frameworks rather than reinventing obligations.

Proposed

Requires 'large frontier developers' to publish a frontier safety framework, report critical safety incidents within 15 days, and publish transparency reports when deploying new or substantially modified frontier models. Whistleblower protections for employees flagging safety issues. The first US state law to codify the published-framework norm — explicitly anchors against Layer 6 lab frameworks rather than reinventing obligations.

ca-sb53coverage · timing
Now

Critical safety incidents must be reported within 15 days; annual transparency reports are required. The 15-day window is the tightest in any US state law.

Proposed

Critical safety incidents must be reported to the Office of Emergency Services within 15 days (24 hours to an appropriate authority if there is an imminent risk of death or serious injury). Transparency reports are due before or with each new or substantially modified frontier model; frameworks are reviewed at least annually; internal-use risk summaries go to OES every three months. NY RAISE's 72-hour window is tighter.

Why it matters

Readers are told SB 53 requires annual transparency reports and has the tightest incident window of any state law; the statute ties transparency reports to deployments, and New York RAISE (72 hours) and Illinois (72 hours) are tighter.

Reasoning

BPC §22757.12(c)(1) requires a transparency report "before, or concurrently with, deploying" a new or substantially modified frontier model; §22757.12(b)(1) sets the annual framework review; §22757.12(d) the three-monthly internal-use summaries; §22757.13(c)(1)–(2) the 15-day and 24-hour incident windows. RAISE §1422(3)(a) sets 72 hours, so 15 days is not the tightest; the map's own ny-raise timing note already says RAISE is tighter.

Uncertainty

None on the statutory text. The sentence about RAISE compares two enacted texts.

Carried over, not re-verified

  • The first US state law to codify the published-framework norm — explicitly anchors against Layer 6 lab frameworks rather than reinventing obligations.

P-0057 v1 changeVerified externally

SB 53 thresholds are tiered: 10²⁶ FLOPs alone triggers transparency and incident duties

accepted v1 · 2026-10-10 · applied 2026-10-10 (2026-10-10-4.json)

Details, evidence and exact wording

Change

ca-sb53coverage · thresh
Now

Eligibility for the law's obligations: cumulative compute >10²⁶ FLOPs and revenue >$500M. Below these thresholds developers are exempt — the law explicitly targets the largest frontier developers, anchoring against Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, Meta, and xAI.

Proposed

Two tiers: 'frontier developers' (training compute >10²⁶ FLOPs, including fine-tuning) must publish transparency reports and report critical safety incidents; 'large frontier developers' (also >$500M revenue) carry the framework, risk-summary and civil-penalty provisions. Developers below 10²⁶ FLOPs are exempt — the law targets the largest frontier developers, anchoring against Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, Meta, and xAI.

Why it matters

The note says developers below the $500M revenue threshold are exempt; the statute imposes transparency-report and incident-reporting duties on every frontier developer above 10²⁶ FLOPs regardless of revenue.

Reasoning

§22757.11(i) defines frontier model by >10²⁶ operations including fine-tuning; (j) adds the $500M revenue test only for large frontier developers. §22757.12(c)(1) (transparency reports) and §22757.13(c)(1) (incidents) apply to "a frontier developer"; §22757.12(a) (framework), (d) (internal-use summaries) and §22757.15 (penalties) apply to "a large frontier developer".

Uncertainty

The named-company list is the existing analytic claim, kept unchanged.

Carried over, not re-verified

  • anchoring against Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, Meta, and xAI

P-0058 v1 changeVerified externally

Colorado SB 26-189 is more than consumer disclosure: developer documentation, human review rights, AG enforcement of rights

accepted v1 · 2026-10-10 · applied 2026-10-10 (2026-10-10-4.json)

Details, evidence and exact wording

Change

co-aiacontext
Now

The original Colorado AI Act would have imposed duty-of-care and algorithmic-impact-assessment duties on developers and deployers of 'high-risk AI systems' for consequential decisions. After federal preemption pressure (xAI litigation, DOJ intervention, April 27 court stay), Colorado repealed the law and replaced it with SB 26-189 — a narrower regime requiring consumer disclosure when AI is used in consequential decisions, without the impact-assessment, duty-of-care, or risk-management obligations of the original. Marks a retreat from the comprehensive state-AI-regulation template.

Proposed

The original Colorado AI Act would have imposed duty-of-care and algorithmic-impact-assessment duties on developers and deployers of 'high-risk AI systems' for consequential decisions. After federal preemption pressure (xAI litigation, DOJ intervention, April 27 court stay), Colorado repealed the law and replaced it with SB 26-189 — a narrower regime of developer documentation, consumer notice, post-adverse-decision explanations and rights to correction and human review when automated decision-making technology is used in consequential decisions, without the impact-assessment, duty-of-care, or risk-management obligations of the original. Marks a retreat from the comprehensive state-AI-regulation template.

co-aiacoverage · mit
Now

Narrower than the original SB 24-205: SB 26-189 requires consumer disclosure when AI is used in consequential decisions but drops the duty of care and impact-assessment regime that drew the federal preemption challenge.

Proposed

Narrower than the original SB 24-205: SB 26-189 requires developer documentation, consumer notice, post-adverse-decision explanations and human review on request when automated decision-making technology is used in consequential decisions, but drops the duty of care and impact-assessment regime that drew the federal preemption challenge.

co-aiacoverage · acct
Now

AG enforcement of disclosure obligations only; the duty-of-care and impact-assessment regime that defined the original Colorado AI Act is gone.

Proposed

AG enforcement of the disclosure duties and consumer rights as deceptive trade practices (60-day cure notice until 2030); no private right of action. The duty-of-care and impact-assessment regime that defined the original Colorado AI Act is gone.

Why it matters

The entry presents SB 26-189 as disclosure-only. The enacted text also obliges developers to document covered systems for deployers and gives consumers correction and human-review rights, which the AG enforces as deceptive trade practices; that matters for the pow classification question.

Reasoning

Chapter 131 (session law) §6-1-1702 (developer documentation), §6-1-1704(1),(3) (notice; 30-day adverse-outcome explanation), §6-1-1705(1)(a)(II) (human review), §6-1-1706(1)(b),(2)(a),(3) (AG-exclusive enforcement of disclosure requirements and consumer rights; deceptive trade practice; 60-day cure, repealed 2030), §6-1-1706(4) (no private right). The repeal of impact assessment, duty of care and risk management is confirmed by their absence from the reenacted part 17.

Uncertainty

Causal framing ("after federal preemption pressure") and "retreat" are analytic; the litigation facts are confirmed by the docket and DOJ release.

Carried over, not re-verified

  • After federal preemption pressure (xAI litigation, DOJ intervention, April 27 court stay), Colorado repealed the law
  • Marks a retreat from the comprehensive state-AI-regulation template.
  • that drew the federal preemption challenge

Now

None.

accepted v1 · 2026-10-10 · applied 2026-10-10 (2026-10-10-4.json)

Details, evidence and exact wording

Change

ny-raisecoverage · acct
Now

Department of Financial Services oversight office — the first US state-level body with dedicated authority over frontier general-purpose AI developers (sectoral AI regulators like the Colorado Division of Insurance, which has overseen insurance-sector algorithms since 2023, predate it). Plus AG enforcement and a public registry of frontier developer frameworks.

Proposed

Department of Financial Services oversight office (DIGIT) — the first US state-level body with dedicated authority over frontier general-purpose AI developers (sectoral AI regulators like the Colorado Division of Insurance, which has overseen insurance-sector algorithms since 2023, predate it). Plus AG enforcement and a published list of large frontier developers that have filed disclosure statements.

Why it matters

The statute does not create a public registry of frameworks: developers publish frameworks on their own websites and the office publishes a list of developers that have filed disclosure statements. The state named the office DIGIT in Sep 2026.

Reasoning

GBL §1421(1) (frameworks on the developer's website), §1428(1),(6) (disclosure statements; office publishes a list of filers), §1429 (office may consider requiring transmission of frameworks to it, so none is required now). The Governor's 21 Sep 2026 release names the office DIGIT within DFS and says registration starts in November 2026.

Uncertainty

The "first US state-level body" claim is comparative and was not verified.

Carried over, not re-verified

  • the first US state-level body with dedicated authority over frontier general-purpose AI developers (sectoral AI regulators like the Colorado Division of Insurance, which has overseen insurance-sector algorithms since 2023, predate it)

P-0067 v1 changeVerified externally

EU AI Office: add the Digital Omnibus powers (Reg. 2026/1744, in force 27 Jul 2026)

accepted v1 · 2026-10-10 · applied 2026-10-10 (2026-10-10-4.json)

Details, evidence and exact wording

Change

eu-aiodesc
Now

Established Jan 2024 within DG CNECT. GPAI enforcement role Aug 2025; full enforcement Aug 2026.

Proposed

Established Jan 2024 within DG CNECT. GPAI enforcement role Aug 2025; full enforcement Aug 2026. Digital Omnibus (Reg. 2026/1744, in force 27 Jul 2026) adds exclusive supervision of AI systems built on a provider's own GPAI model and of AI in very large online platforms and search engines.

eu-aiocontext
Now

Coordinates AI Act implementation across member states, enforces GPAI obligations directly (a centralised role unique within EU regulatory architecture), and runs the Scientific Panel that advises on systemic risk. Can request models from providers, order recalls, and impose fines. Effectively the EU's frontier-AI regulator; partner of the AISI Network despite being an EU body rather than a national one.

Proposed

Coordinates AI Act implementation across member states, enforces GPAI obligations directly (a centralised role unique within EU regulatory architecture), and runs the Scientific Panel that advises on systemic risk. Can request models from providers, order recalls, and impose fines; since the Omnibus it also has market-surveillance powers over the AI systems it supervises, including on-site inspections, binding commitments and fines (new AI Act Arts 75a–75d). Effectively the EU's frontier-AI regulator; partner of the AISI Network despite being an EU body rather than a national one.

Why it matters

The map describes the AI Office as a GPAI-only enforcer. Since 27 July 2026 it is also the exclusive supervisor of GPAI-based AI systems built by the model's own provider (e.g. a lab's own chatbot) and of AI in VLOPs/VLOSEs, with inspection and fining powers. That is a material expansion of the frontier-relevant regulator's remit.

Reasoning

Reg. (EU) 2026/1744 Art. 1(31) replaces AI Act Art. 75(1) to make the AI Office 'exclusively competent' for (a) AI systems based on GPAI models where model and system come from the same provider/undertaking and (b) AI systems that constitute or are integrated into a VLOP/VLOSE (omnibus p3–p5). New Art. 75a(4) gives remote/on-site inspections (p6); Art. 75c(4) penalties (p7); Art. 75b binding commitments. Entry into force on the third day after OJ publication of 24.7.2026 = 27 July 2026 (p2, p8), confirmed by the Commission's AI Office page (ec-aio p2). The Commission's enforcement page summarises the same scope (ec-enforcement p1–p2, p7). Existing desc facts re-checked: Commission Decision of 24 Jan 2024 placing the Office in DG CNECT (aio-decision p1–p2); Chapter V GPAI obligations apply from 2 Aug 2025 (ai-act p6); enforcement powers from 2 Aug 2026 (ec-enforcement p6).

Uncertainty

Some exceptions apply to Art. 75(1)(a) (Annex I products, critical infrastructure, law enforcement/border/financial institutions, justice); the desc omits them for brevity. The Commission page says the omnibus was 'adopted' in June 2026, while the Regulation is dated 8 July 2026 (signature); the proposal avoids an adoption date.

Carried over, not re-verified

  • context: 'a centralised role unique within EU regulatory architecture'
  • context: 'Effectively the EU's frontier-AI regulator'

caisidesc

Renamed from US AISI in Jun 2025. Within NIST. Mission rewritten to drop "safety" framing, but active pre-deployment testing capacity returned in 2026.

Proposed

Renamed from US AISI in Jun 2025. Within NIST. Mission rewritten to drop "safety" framing, but active pre-deployment testing capacity returned in 2026. Relabelled Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence (CAISSI) on NIST's site after EO 14434 (29 Sep 2026) replaced "AI" with "Super Intelligence" in executive-branch usage.

caisilink
Now

https://www.nist.gov/caisi

Proposed

https://www.nist.gov/caissi

Why it matters

Readers following the link land on a page titled 'Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence (CAISSI)', which the map never mentions. The change follows a presidential order that governs executive-branch terminology, so it is likely to persist.

Reasoning

EO 14434 §1 makes it policy that the executive branch 'shall use the terms Super Intelligence and SI in place of Artificial Intelligence and AI' and §2(a) applies this to agency 'websites' (eo14434 p2–p3; signed 29 Sep 2026, published 2 Oct 2026). NIST's page, modified 30 Sep 2026, is now titled CAISSI and describes the same mission in SI terms, including voluntary agreements with developers and unclassified national-security evaluations (nist-caissi p1–p3, p5). The old /caisi URL redirects to /caissi (p5). The Jun 2025 rename is confirmed by NIST (nist-news p1).

Uncertainty

NIST has not issued a separate notice of the rename; the link to EO 14434 is inferred from timing and the order's text. NIST news items before 30 Sep 2026 still say 'CAISI'. Whether to relabel the entry name is raised separately (caisi-name-flag).

Carried over, not re-verified

  • desc: 'Mission rewritten to drop "safety" framing, but active pre-deployment testing capacity returned in 2026' (the 2026 pre-deployment claim rests on the 5 May 2026 agreements announcement, which NIST has since removed; see check on entry:caisi:context)

Proposed

National-level frontier model testing varies substantially: Singapore's DTC + AI Verify package is the most operational; J-AISI focuses on standards alignment; INESIA is building national evaluation capacity. India and Africa are still scaling.

Why it matters

The entry says all these institutes are coordinated through the AISI Network, but India is not a member; and it credits INESIA with EU-wide tooling that no source describes.

Reasoning

The Network's member list (Dec 2025 GOV.UK release linked from this entry, and the Jul 2026 AISI blog after the Seoul meeting) names Australia, Canada, the EU, France, Japan, Kenya, Korea, Singapore, the UK and the US, not India (govuk-network p1; aisi-seoul p1). India's institute exists (in-aisi p1). INESIA's own 2026–27 roadmap release describes it as led by DGE and SGDSN, federating ANSSI, Inria, LNE and PEReN, to give France a 'sovereign' evaluation capacity (inesia p1–p4).

Uncertainty

The 'EU-wide tooling' claim may refer to something not found here (e.g. a project hosted by an INESIA member); absence on the roadmap page does not prove it false. The network has been renamed the International Network for Advanced AI Measurement, Evaluation and Science (govuk-network p2); the proposal keeps the map's 'AISI Network' label, which belongs to the aisi-net entry.

Carried over, not re-verified

  • 'J-AISI focuses on standards alignment'

P-0073 v1 changeVerified externally

FSI ↔ US Frontier AI Access EO: the order creates a voluntary access framework, not a national-security review

accepted v1 · 2026-10-10 · applied 2026-10-10 (2026-10-10-4.json)

Details, evidence and exact wording

Change

fsi ↔ us-frontier-access-eoconnection
Now

FSI's policy translation aligns with the EO's national-security review framework

Proposed

FSI's lab–national-security translation bears on the EO's voluntary frontier-model access framework

Why it matters

The connection repeats the framing the map already corrected in the EO entry (P-0014): EO 14409 sets up voluntary, cyber-focused access and expressly rules out preclearance; there is no 'review framework'.

Reasoning

EO 14409 §3(a) creates a classified cyber benchmarking process; §3(b) a 'voluntary framework' through which developers may give the government access to covered frontier models for up to 30 days before release to other trusted partners; §3(c) excludes any mandatory licensing or preclearance (eo14409 p1–p4). FSI describes itself as a translation layer between labs and the National Security Enterprise (cais-fsi p7; fsi-home p1).

Uncertainty

The relationship is editorial in either wording; FSI's pages do not mention the order. Removing the connection is a reasonable alternative.

P-0075 v1 changeVerified externally

BIS: record the unenforced AI Diffusion Rule and the 2026 H200 licensing change; fix the misdated compute-tier claim

accepted v1 · 2026-10-10 · applied 2026-10-10 (2026-10-10-4.json)

Details, evidence and exact wording

Change

bisdesc
Now

Bureau of Industry and Security chip export rules (2022, 2023, 2024). Most consequential single piece — shapes who can train at the frontier.

Proposed

Bureau of Industry and Security chip export rules (2022, 2023, 2024). The Jan 2025 AI Diffusion Rule (country tiers, model-weight controls) has not been enforced since May 2025; a Jan 2026 rule moved licences for H200-class chips to China to case-by-case review. Most consequential single piece — shapes who can train at the frontier.

biscontext
Now

Successive rules tightened export-licence requirements for advanced compute (GPUs, fabrication tools, lithography) to China and other concerns; the 2024 update added compute-tier thresholds tied to model-training scale. May 31, 2026 guidance closed a key loophole by confirming the ultimate-parent-company test applies — any subsidiary worldwide whose ultimate parent is in the restricted countries list needs a US license. Operates outside the safety-regulation framing — its lever is who can build frontier models at all, not what they must do once built. The single most consequential piece of US AI policy by impact, even though it isn't framed as 'AI regulation.'

Proposed

Successive rules tightened export-licence requirements for advanced compute (GPUs, fabrication tools, lithography) to China and other concerns; the Dec 2024 update added controls on high-bandwidth memory and chipmaking equipment. The Jan 2025 AI Diffusion Rule added country tiers and a licence requirement for closed model weights trained on more than 10²⁶ operations, but BIS stopped enforcing it in May 2025 and said it would rescind and replace it. May 31, 2026 guidance closed a key loophole by confirming the ultimate-parent-company test applies — any subsidiary worldwide whose ultimate parent is in the restricted countries list needs a US license. Operates outside the safety-regulation framing — its lever is who can build frontier models at all, not what they must do once built. The single most consequential piece of US AI policy by impact, even though it isn't framed as 'AI regulation.'

biscoverage · thresh
Now

Compute thresholds tied to model-training scale govern export-licence requirements for advanced GPUs, fabrication tools, and lithography. The 2024 update introduced an explicit framework tying export controls to AI capability.

Proposed

Chip-performance thresholds (total processing performance) govern export-licence requirements for advanced GPUs; separate controls cover fabrication tools and lithography. The Jan 2025 AI Diffusion Rule's model-weight threshold (more than 10²⁶ training operations) is not being enforced.

Why it matters

The entry says the 2024 rule tied export controls to model-training scale and is silent on the 2025 rescission and the 2026 loosening for China, so a reader gets the wrong picture of what US controls currently do to frontier training and model weights.

Reasoning

The Dec 2024 rule (89 FR 96790) added HBM, SME and FDP controls, not compute tiers. The tiered framework and the >10^26-operation model-weight control came in the Jan 2025 AI Diffusion IFR (90 FR 4544). BIS announced on 13 May 2025 that it would not enforce that rule and would formalise rescission and issue a replacement; the July 2026 UAE rule confirms BIS still enforces the worldwide licence requirement only for D:1/D:4/D:5 destinations and D:5/Macau-headquartered entities, consistent with the May 2025 and May 2026 guidance. The Jan 2026 final rule moved H200-class (TPP < 21,000) exports to China/Macau from presumption of denial to case-by-case review. Chip controls are keyed to TPP, not model-training scale.

Uncertainty

No Federal Register rule formally rescinding the AI Diffusion Rule was found as of 10 Oct 2026 (FR API search); if one is published, "has not been enforced" should become "rescinded". The "fabrication tools and lithography" wording is carried over.

Carried over, not re-verified

  • "Most consequential single piece — shapes who can train at the frontier"
  • "separate controls cover fabrication tools and lithography" (from the existing note)
  • rest of the context, including the closing analytic sentences

P-0077 v1 changeVerified externally

US FTC: Rytr order set aside; FTC now aligned with, not in tension with, the preemption EO

accepted v1 · 2026-10-10 · applied 2026-10-10 (2026-10-10-4.json)

Details, evidence and exact wording

Change

us-ftccontext
Now

Active enforcement against deceptive AI claims and harmful AI deployments under existing consumer-protection authority. Operation AI Comply (Sept 2024) brought five cases against AI hype, fake reviews, and unsubstantiated claims; the Rite Aid biometric AI case (2024) banned facial recognition use for five years. Less direct frontier-developer relevance than the EU AI Office, but shapes deployment practice through enforcement signals. Operates in some tension with the DOJ Litigation Task Force — DOJ challenges state AI rules while FTC enforces federal consumer law against AI.

Proposed

Active enforcement against deceptive AI claims and harmful AI deployments under existing consumer-protection authority. Operation AI Comply (Sept 2024) brought five cases against AI hype, fake reviews, and unsubstantiated claims (the current Commission set aside the Rytr order in Dec 2025 as an unnecessary burden on AI innovation); the Rite Aid biometric AI case (2024) banned facial recognition use for five years. Less direct frontier-developer relevance than the EU AI Office, but shapes deployment practice through enforcement signals. Now enlisted in the federal preemption push: EO 14365 directed it to explain when Section 5 preempts state laws requiring altered AI outputs, and its July 2026 proposed policy statement says such laws are impliedly preempted where they require deception.

us-ftc ↔ us-preemptconnection
Now

FTC's AI enforcement operates in tension with DOJ Task Force's preemption challenges

Proposed

EO 14365 directs the FTC to explain when Section 5 preempts state AI-output laws; FTC proposed that policy statement in Jul 2026

Why it matters

The entry and connection present the FTC as a counterweight to DOJ's preemption campaign, but the preemption EO itself tasks the FTC with a preemption policy statement, which the FTC has now proposed; and one of the five Operation AI Comply orders has been withdrawn.

Reasoning

EO 14365 Sec. 7 orders the FTC Chairman to issue a policy statement explaining when state laws requiring alterations to truthful AI outputs are preempted by the FTC Act. The FTC published that proposed statement on 7 Jul 2026 (comments to 31 Jul 2026); it cites EO 14365 as its mandate and states that state law is impliedly preempted where it conflicts with Section 5. The same document records that the Commission set aside the Rytr order on 22 Dec 2025 to address "unnecessary burdens".

Uncertainty

The policy statement is still a proposal; no final version was found in the Federal Register as of 10 Oct 2026. The Rite Aid sentence is carried over unverified (ftc.gov refuses automated clients).

Carried over, not re-verified

  • Operation AI Comply "five cases" (Sept 2024)
  • Rite Aid biometric AI case (2024) and five-year ban
  • "Less direct frontier-developer relevance than the EU AI Office..." (analytic)

P-0078 v1 changeVerified externally

UK Ofcom: illegal-content duties are not limited to Category 1; codes have no AI-specific provisions; 2026 power to extend the Act to AI services

accepted v1 · 2026-10-10 · applied 2026-10-10 (2026-10-10-4.json)

Details, evidence and exact wording

Change

uk-ofcomcontext
Now

Originally telecoms and broadcasting regulator; the Online Safety Act 2023 added enforcement authority over AI-generated harmful content (deepfakes, non-consensual intimate imagery, CSAM, fraud) on Category 1 services. The Illegal Content Codes of Practice (2025) include AI-specific provisions for image-generation safeguards and content authentication. Shapes how labs ship image/video generators into the UK market, even though it doesn't target frontier developers directly.

Proposed

Originally telecoms and broadcasting regulator; the Online Safety Act 2023 added enforcement authority over illegal content, including AI-generated harmful content (deepfakes, non-consensual intimate imagery, CSAM, fraud), on regulated user-to-user and search services, with extra duties for Category 1 services. The Illegal Content Codes of Practice (in force Mar 2025) recommend measures such as CSAM hash matching but contain no AI-specific provisions. The Crime and Policing Act 2026 lets the Secretary of State extend the Act's illegal-content duties and Ofcom's enforcement powers to AI services, such as chatbots, by regulations. Shapes how labs ship image/video generators into the UK market, even though it doesn't target frontier developers directly.

uk-ofcomcoverage · mit
Now

Codes of Practice require content authentication, age verification, and safeguards on AI-generated harmful content for in-scope services.

Proposed

Codes of Practice recommend (rather than mandate) measures such as CSAM hash matching and swift takedown, plus age assurance under the children's codes; an NCII hash-matching measure was added in 2026. Following them counts as compliance. No AI-specific measures such as content authentication.

Why it matters

The entry overstates the AI-specificity of Ofcom's codes and misstates who the illegal-content duties bind, while missing the 2026 statutory power that would bring generative-AI services directly under Ofcom.

Reasoning

OSA s.7(2) applies the illegal-content duties to all regulated user-to-user services (Category 1 adds further duties, s.7(5)); the EM confirms the duties cover search services too (s.27). A full-text search of the user-to-user Illegal content Codes found no AI, generative, deepfake, provenance, authentication or watermark measure; the codes recommend CSAM hash matching (ICU C9) and swift takedown (ICU C2.3), and the EM states their measures are not mandatory but compliance is presumed when followed. The 2026 amendment adds NCII hash matching. Crime and Policing Act 2026 s.248 (in force at Royal Assent) inserts OSA s.216A, letting the Secretary of State extend illegal-content duties and Ofcom's enforcement and penalty powers to "AI services"; the government presented this as closing the AI-chatbot loophole.

Uncertainty

No regulations under the new s.216A had been made as of 10 Oct 2026 (legislation.gov.uk title search). The NCII amendment's exact in-force date was not confirmed (Ofcom's site refuses automated clients); age assurance under the children's codes is carried over unverified.

Carried over, not re-verified

  • "Originally telecoms and broadcasting regulator"
  • the list of harms (deepfakes, NCII, CSAM, fraud)
  • age assurance under the children's codes
  • closing analytic sentence

P-0079 v1 changeVerified externally

UK ICO: replaced by the Information Commission (30 Sep 2026); AI guidance is non-statutory, not binding

accepted v1 · 2026-10-10 · applied 2026-10-10 (2026-10-10-4.json)

Details, evidence and exact wording

Change

uk-icodesc
Now

Information Commissioner's Office — data protection regulator with binding AI guidance under UK GDPR. Fines up to £17.5M or 4% of global revenue.

Proposed

Information Commission (took over from the Information Commissioner on 30 Sep 2026; still branded ICO) — data protection regulator applying UK GDPR to AI, with non-statutory AI guidance. Fines up to £17.5M or 4% of global turnover.

uk-icocontext
Now

Regulates how organisations train on, deploy, and explain AI under UK GDPR. The AI Auditing Framework (2020, updated 2023) and the Guidance on AI and Data Protection set binding expectations for lawful basis, fairness, transparency, and Data Protection Impact Assessments for AI systems. Has investigated Clearview AI, Snap My AI, and others — operates as the UK's de facto frontier-AI privacy regulator alongside any future AISI statutory mandate.

Proposed

Regulates how organisations train on, deploy, and explain AI under UK GDPR. Its Guidance on AI and Data Protection (2020, updated 2023), part of its AI auditing framework, sets out how it interprets the law on lawful basis, fairness, transparency, and Data Protection Impact Assessments for AI systems; it is not a statutory code and is under review after the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025. Has investigated Clearview AI, Snap My AI, and others — operates as the UK's de facto frontier-AI privacy regulator alongside any future AISI statutory mandate.

uk-icocoverage · mit
Now

Binding guidance on fairness, transparency, lawful basis, and explainability for AI deployments touching personal data.

Proposed

Non-statutory guidance on fairness, transparency, lawful basis, and explainability for AI deployments touching personal data; the underlying UK GDPR duties are binding.

Why it matters

The entry calls the ICO's AI guidance binding, which the ICO itself denies, and names an office that was abolished on 30 Sep 2026.

Reasoning

The ICO's guidance says it "is not a statutory code" and that there is "no penalty if you fail to adopt good practice recommendations" provided the law is otherwise complied with; it is under review after the DUAA. The guidance is one of three outputs of the AI auditing framework, not a separate instrument. DUAA 2025 s.118 abolished the office of Information Commissioner and s.119 transferred its functions to the Information Commission, both in force 30 Sep 2026 (SI 2026/1015). The website still uses the ICO name. Penalty cap confirmed in DPA 2018 s.157(5).

Uncertainty

Whether to rename the entry (e.g. "UK Information Commission (ICO)") is left to the maintainer; the brand is still ICO. The 2020/2023 guidance dates and the Clearview reference are carried over.

Carried over, not re-verified

  • "(2020, updated 2023)"
  • Clearview AI investigation
  • "operates as the UK's de facto frontier-AI privacy regulator..." (analytic)

P-0080 v1 changeVerified externally

Australia eSafety: update the penalty figure (30,000 penalty units for codes/standards)

accepted v1 · 2026-10-10 · applied 2026-10-10 (2026-10-10-4.json)

Details, evidence and exact wording

Change

au-esafetycontext
Now

Issues binding industry Codes and Standards (including for AI-generated content) under the Online Safety Act 2021. The 2024 Industry Standards mandate proactive safeguards against AI-generated CSAM and pro-terror material from Designated Internet Services. Takedown powers, civil penalties up to AUD 782,500 per contravention, and business-disruption orders. The leading non-EU model for AI-content regulation with binding effect; influences regulatory templates in the Five Eyes and broader Asia-Pacific.

Proposed

Issues binding industry Codes and Standards (including for AI-generated content) under the Online Safety Act 2021. The 2024 Industry Standards mandate proactive safeguards against AI-generated CSAM and pro-terror material from Designated Internet Services. Takedown powers, civil penalties of up to 30,000 penalty units for breaching an industry standard or a direction to comply with a code (500 for most notice breaches), and business-disruption orders. The leading non-EU model for AI-content regulation with binding effect; influences regulatory templates in the Five Eyes and broader Asia-Pacific.

au-esafetycoverage · acct
Now

Civil penalties up to AUD 782,500 per contravention; takedown notices; service-disruption orders.

Proposed

Civil penalties of up to 30,000 penalty units for breaching an industry standard or a code direction (500 for most notice breaches); takedown notices; service-disruption orders.

Why it matters

AUD 782,500 reflects the old 500-penalty-unit cap; breaches of the industry standards that carry the AI-specific obligations now attract up to 30,000 penalty units.

Reasoning

The current compilation of the Online Safety Act 2021 (No. 4, 12 Sep 2026) sets 30,000 penalty units for contravening a registered industry standard (s.146) and for failing to comply with a direction to comply with an industry code (s.143(2)); removal-notice and similar notice breaches remain at 500 penalty units (e.g. s.67).

Uncertainty

The dollar value depends on the Commonwealth penalty unit and on corporate multipliers under the Regulatory Powers Act, so the proposal states penalty units rather than dollars. "Business-disruption orders" is carried over unverified.

Carried over, not re-verified

  • business-disruption / service-disruption orders
  • "The leading non-EU model..." (analytic)

Evidence

P-0086 v2 changeVerified externally

Japan sectoral AI regulators: keep, anchored on the MIC/METI AI Guidelines for Business

accepted v2 · 2026-10-11 · applied 2026-10-11 (2026-10-11.json)

Details, evidence and exact wording

Revised from v1: wording changed, so it needs a fresh decision.

Change

jp-sectorsdesc
Now

Sectoral AI guidance from Japan's ministry regulators (METI, FSA, MHLW, MIC) under the AI Promotion Act framework. Soft guidance rather than binding rules.

Proposed

Sectoral AI guidance from Japan's ministries under the AI Promotion Act framework, anchored by the MIC/METI AI Guidelines for Business (v1.2, Mar 2026), which call themselves soft law without legally binding force.

jp-sectorscontext
Now

Japan's AI governance operates sector-by-sector: METI (Economy, Trade and Industry) issues the AI Guidelines for Business and developer-facing principles; FSA (Financial Services Agency) handles AI risk management in finance; MHLW (Health, Labour and Welfare) covers AI in healthcare and employment; MIC (Internal Affairs and Communications) governs AI in telecoms and media. Coordinated through the AI Strategic Headquarters under the Cabinet Office. The deliberately soft approach — voluntary guidelines, no compute thresholds, no fines — mirrors the Hiroshima Process Japan championed at the G7.

Proposed

Japan's AI governance operates sector-by-sector: METI (Economy, Trade and Industry) and MIC jointly issue the AI Guidelines for Business, the main cross-sector instrument; FSA (Financial Services Agency) handles AI risk management in finance; MHLW (Health, Labour and Welfare) covers AI in healthcare and employment; MIC (Internal Affairs and Communications) governs AI in telecoms and media. Coordinated through the AI Strategic Headquarters under the Cabinet Office. The deliberately soft approach — voluntary guidelines, no compute thresholds, no fines — mirrors the Hiroshima Process Japan championed at the G7.

Why it matters

RUBRIC §1 requires an identifiable instrument and an attributable actor; an aggregate of ministries satisfies neither cleanly. SCOPE §C asks for this to be raised.

Reasoning

The question had no stated recommendation, so this is mine: keep the entry but anchor it on the one specific, citable instrument (the question's middle option), and correct the context that credited the Guidelines to METI alone. From the Guidelines' cover and preface (S-0267#1, S-0267#2).

Uncertainty

The FSA and MHLW roles in the context are carried over, not verified.

P-0087 v1 changeVerified externally

US EO 14179: it followed EO 14148's revocation of EO 14110 and ordered rescission of actions under it; it did not itself rescind red-teaming, reporting or voluntary commitments

accepted v1 · 2026-10-10 · applied 2026-10-10 (2026-10-10-4.json)

Details, evidence and exact wording

Change

us-eo14179desc
Now

Trump (Jan 2025) replaced Biden EO 14110. Rescinded mandatory red-teaming and pre-deployment reporting.

Proposed

Trump (Jan 23, 2025). Issued after EO 14148 revoked Biden EO 14110, whose reporting duties covered red-team results for dual-use foundation models; orders agencies to suspend, revise or rescind actions taken under EO 14110.

us-eo14179context
Now

Frames AI policy as removing regulatory barriers to American leadership; ordered the AI Action Plan within 180 days. Withdrew the safety-focused infrastructure of the prior administration — voluntary commitments, mandatory red-teaming, pre-deployment reporting. Marks the federal turn away from safety-oriented governance toward an industrial-policy framing.

Proposed

Frames AI policy as removing regulatory barriers to American leadership; ordered the AI Action Plan within 180 days. Ordered review and rescission of the safety-focused measures taken under EO 14110, such as reporting of red-team results for dual-use foundation models. Marks the federal turn away from safety-oriented governance toward an industrial-policy framing.

Why it matters

Readers take the entry to say EO 14179 itself rescinded mandatory red-teaming, pre-deployment reporting and the voluntary commitments. The revocation of EO 14110 was done by EO 14148 three days earlier. EO 14110 required reporting of red-team results, not red-teaming as such. The 2023 voluntary commitments were never part of either order.

Reasoning

EO 14148 §2(ggg) revokes EO 14110. EO 14179 refers to 'the revoked Executive Order 14110' and orders agencies to suspend, revise or rescind actions taken under it (§5(a)). EO 14110 §4.2(a)(i)(C) required companies to report red-team test results. EO 14179 never mentions red-teaming, reporting or voluntary commitments.

Uncertainty

'Replaced' in the current desc is loose rather than wrong. The proposal names the revoking order precisely.

Carried over, not re-verified

  • Marks the federal turn away from safety-oriented governance toward an industrial-policy framing.

Now

EU AI Act · Updating: the Commission can revise the 10²⁵ threshold and the Annex III list by delegated act

accepted v1 · 2026-10-10 · applied 2026-10-10 (2026-10-10-4.json)

Details, evidence and exact wording

Change

eu-aiacoverage · update
Now

The Code of Practice and harmonised standards are revisable as the field changes; the underlying regulation is amendable through ordinary EU legislative procedure (slower).

Proposed

The Code of Practice and harmonised standards are revisable as the field changes, and the Commission can update the 10²⁵ threshold and the Annex III high-risk list by delegated act; other changes to the regulation go through ordinary EU legislative procedure (slower).

Why it matters

Read for the METR 'updating' element, the note suggests the regulation changes only through ordinary legislation. The Act has a faster built-in route for its key threshold and high-risk list.

Reasoning

Art. 51(3) obliges the Commission to adopt delegated acts amending the systemic-risk thresholds as technology evolves. Art. 7(1) lets it amend Annex III. Art. 56(8) provides for review of the codes.

Uncertainty

Whether this omission is material enough to change is a judgment.

P-0099 v1 changeVerified externally

China GenAI Measures: security assessment and algorithm filing apply only to services with public-opinion or mobilisation capacity; no 'licensed intermediary' rule; the CAC publishes filings, not approvals

accepted v1 · 2026-10-10 · applied 2026-10-10 (2026-10-10-4.json)

Details, evidence and exact wording

Change

cn-genaicontext
Now

Requires algorithm registration with the Cyberspace Administration of China before public deployment, security assessment of training data, and content moderation aligned with Chinese law. Foreign-trained models can serve Chinese users only via licensed domestic intermediaries. Enforcement is active — multiple firms have had services suspended — but operates as much through industrial policy as through fines.

Proposed

Services with public-opinion attributes or social-mobilisation capacity must undergo a security assessment and file their algorithms with the Cyberspace Administration of China; all providers must use lawfully sourced training data and moderate content in line with Chinese law. Non-compliant services offered from outside China can be blocked. Enforcement is active — multiple firms have had services suspended — but operates as much through industrial policy as through fines.

cn-genaicoverage · timing
Now

Pre-deployment security assessment is mandatory for any generative AI service offered to the Chinese public; the Cyberspace Administration of China reviews training data, model behaviour, and content controls before approval.

Proposed

Services with public-opinion attributes or social-mobilisation capacity must undergo a security assessment under national rules and complete algorithm filing with the Cyberspace Administration of China (Art. 17); apps built on them must display the filing number.

cn-genaicoverage · mit
Now

Content moderation aligned with Chinese law (including political-content rules), training-data security assessment, and labelling of AI-generated outputs are required. Concrete deployment rules with active enforcement — multiple firms have had services suspended.

Proposed

Content moderation aligned with Chinese law (including political-content rules), training-data rules (lawful sources, IP, consent, quality), and labelling of AI-generated outputs are required. Concrete deployment rules with active enforcement — multiple firms have had services suspended.

cn-genaicoverage · acct
Now

Algorithm registration with the Cyberspace Administration is mandatory before public deployment. The CAC maintains a public registry of approved algorithms; foreign-trained models can serve Chinese users only via licensed domestic intermediaries.

Proposed

Services with public-opinion attributes or social-mobilisation capacity must file their algorithms with the Cyberspace Administration (Art. 17); the CAC publishes lists of filed generative AI services. Non-compliant services offered from outside China can be blocked (Art. 20).

Why it matters

The entry says a security assessment and registration are required for every public generative AI service, and that foreign models need licensed domestic intermediaries. Art. 17 limits both duties to services with public-opinion attributes or social-mobilisation capacity. The Measures contain no intermediary rule. The CAC registry lists filings, not approvals.

Reasoning

Art. 17 sets the scope. Art. 7 covers training-data duties (lawful sources, IP, consent, quality), not a training-data security assessment. Art. 12 requires labelling. Art. 20 provides for blocking non-compliant offshore services. The CAC's announcement publishes 'filed' (已备案) services and requires apps to display the filing number.

Uncertainty

In practice the CAC applies filing broadly to public-facing models, and the TC260 standard used in filing includes training-data security checks. The proposal states the legal text.

Carried over, not re-verified

  • Enforcement is active — multiple firms have had services suspended — but operates as much through industrial policy as through fines.
  • Concrete deployment rules with active enforcement — multiple firms have had services suspended.

Details, evidence and exact wording

Change

Proposed

The 2024 King's Speech promised legislation on developers of the most powerful AI models; no government bill was introduced, and the May 2026 King's Speech announced none.

uk-billlink

Why it matters

Bill 3942 is Lord Holmes's Artificial Intelligence (Regulation) Bill [HL], a Conservative private member's bill. It had only a first reading (4 Mar 2025) and was not carried into the 2026-27 session. The government's own bill was never introduced, and the 13 May 2026 King's Speech does not include it.

Reasoning

The 2024 King's Speech text contains the commitment. The Bills API shows bill 3942's sponsor and its single stage in session 39 only (a carried-over bill shows sessions 39 and 40). A search for 'artificial intelligence' finds no government bill. The 2026 speech and briefing notes mention AI only as sandboxes in a Regulating for Growth Bill.

Uncertainty

Ministers may still promise frontier legislation later; nothing official is public.

Conducts pre-deployment evaluations of frontier models under voluntary access agreements with major labs; publishes red-teaming and jailbreaking research. Proposed

Conducts pre-deployment evaluations of frontier models under voluntary access agreements with major labs; publishes red-teaming and jailbreaking research. The Feb 2025 rename to 'AI Security Institute' narrowed focus toward national-security-adjacent risks (cyber, bio, autonomy) and aligned framing with US CAISI. The 2024 King's Speech promised legislation on developers of the most powerful AI models, but no government bill was introduced and the May 2026 King's Speech announced none, so its access remains voluntary — labs could withdraw. The inaugural Frontier AI Trends Report (Dec 2025) draws on two years of evaluating 30+ frontier models.

Why it matters

The entry presents an inactive, textless proposal as a live bill.

Reasoning

(a) applies RUBRIC §1 strictly: a proposed law needs a formally introduced bill or a programme with public text or consultation, and there is neither. (b) keeps the history visible as its own entry. Both remove the unverified 'would clarify' connections; under (b) the AISI connection is reworded as an expectation. Evidence: King's Speech 2024 (S-0286#1), King's Speech 2026 and briefing notes (S-0287#2, S-0288#2), and Lord Holmes's private member's bill stalled at first reading (S-0282#2, S-0283#2). Maintainer chose option a (the recommended option).

Uncertainty

Removing the entry lowers the mechanism count by one; the derived counts update automatically.

P-0102 v1 changeVerified externally

Korea AI Basic Act: the Enforcement Decree adds capability and risk criteria to the 10²⁶ FLOPs threshold

accepted v1 · 2026-10-10 · applied 2026-10-10 (2026-10-10-4.json)

Details, evidence and exact wording

Change

kr-aicoverage · thresh
Now

Defines high-performance AI as cumulative compute ≥10²⁶ FLOPs (matching California SB 53 and NY RAISE, higher than the EU AI Act's 10²⁵). High-impact AI is defined separately by use-case rather than compute.

Proposed

The Act's safety duties (Art. 32) cover systems above a compute threshold set by decree. The Enforcement Decree (Art. 24, in force Jan 22, 2026) requires cumulative compute ≥10²⁶ FLOPs (matching California SB 53 and NY RAISE, higher than the EU AI Act's 10²⁵) plus state-of-the-art technology and risks with broad, serious effects on life, safety and fundamental rights. High-impact AI is defined separately by use-case rather than compute.

kr-aicontext
Now

Korea's first horizontal AI law: tiered obligations on high-impact AI and high-performance AI (≥10²⁶ FLOPs), risk management plans, lifecycle reporting to MSIT, mandatory generative-AI labelling, and a state AI Safety Research Institute. Penalty caps are deliberately low — the Act emphasises guidance over deterrence, mirroring Japan's approach and contrasting with the EU's prescriptive route.

Proposed

Korea's first horizontal AI law: tiered obligations on high-impact AI and high-performance AI (≥10²⁶ FLOPs plus capability and risk criteria), risk management plans, lifecycle reporting to MSIT, mandatory generative-AI labelling, and a state AI Safety Research Institute. Penalty caps are deliberately low — the Act emphasises guidance over deterrence, mirroring Japan's approach and contrasting with the EU's prescriptive route.

Why it matters

Compute alone does not trigger the duties. The decree's three criteria are cumulative, so fewer models are covered than a pure 10²⁶ test would suggest.

Reasoning

Act Art. 32(1) delegates the compute standard to Presidential Decree. Decree Art. 24(1) requires all of: ≥10^26 FLOPs, most-advanced technology, and broad, serious risk. Decree Addenda Art. 1 sets entry into force on 22 Jan 2026.

Uncertainty

MSIT's notice on how compute is calculated (Decree Art. 24(2)) was not inspected.

Carried over, not re-verified

  • matching California SB 53 and NY RAISE
  • Penalty caps are deliberately low — the Act emphasises guidance over deterrence, mirroring Japan's approach and contrasting with the EU's prescriptive route.

P-0103 v1 changeVerified externally

Korea AI Basic Act · Accountability: oversight sits with MSIT; the AI Safety Research Institute supports rather than oversees

accepted v1 · 2026-10-10 · applied 2026-10-10 (2026-10-10-4.json)

Details, evidence and exact wording

Change

kr-aicoverage · acct
Now

Notification duties to MSIT, oversight by the new AI Safety Research Institute, and user complaint mechanisms. Enforcement teeth deliberately weak — penalty caps ~$21k per violation.

Proposed

Safety-duty results go to MSIT, which can investigate (including on reports or complaints) and order violations stopped or corrected (Art. 40); the AI Safety Research Institute supports safety work rather than overseeing it. Enforcement teeth deliberately weak — fines capped at ₩30M (~$21k) (Art. 43).

Why it matters

The note credits the AI Safety Research Institute with oversight. Under the Act the Institute is a research and support body that MSIT 'may operate'. Investigation and corrective orders belong to MSIT.

Reasoning

Art. 12 lists the Institute's tasks: research, standards, international cooperation and support for Art. 32 safety. Art. 32(2) requires results to be submitted to MSIT. Art. 40 gives MSIT investigation (triggered by findings, reports or complaints) and stop or correct orders. Art. 43 caps fines at KRW 30M.

Uncertainty

Low.

Carried over, not re-verified

  • Enforcement teeth deliberately weak

Change

jp-aicoverage · mit
Now

Sectoral guidance issued by the AI Strategic Headquarters under the Cabinet Office, with each sector regulator translating high-level principles into industry-specific expectations. No horizontal deployment rules.

Proposed

Non-binding AI guidelines under Art. 13, adopted by the AI Strategic Headquarters in Dec 2025, alongside ministries' own sectoral guidance (e.g. the AI Business Guidelines), with each sector regulator translating high-level principles into industry-specific expectations. No binding deployment rules.

Why it matters

The note says the AI Strategic HQ issues sectoral guidance. What the HQ actually adopted is a single cross-cutting guideline under Art. 13. Sector-specific guidance comes from individual ministries.

Reasoning

Art. 13 requires guidelines consistent with international norms. The Cabinet Office page shows the HQ's decision of 19 Dec 2025 and lists ministry guidelines such as the AI Business Guidelines.

Uncertainty

The guidelines themselves were not read in full.

P-0106 v1 additionVerified externally

New entry: US FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925), a bipartisan federal frontier-AI bill with state preemption

accepted v1 · 2026-10-10 · applied 2026-10-10 (2026-10-10-4.json)

Details, evidence and exact wording

Change

us-frontier-actnew entry · Layer 2 · us · pow 2 · proposed

US FRONTIER Act

https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-119hr9925ih/html/BILLS-119hr9925ih.htm

H.R. 9925, bipartisan House bill introduced Jul 23, 2026 (Obernolte, Trahan). Frontier models >10²⁶ FLOPs: published frameworks, annual third-party audits, 72-hour incident reports, licensed verifiers for the largest developers; up to $1M per violation. Would preempt state frontier-transparency, audit and incident-reporting rules.

Would create a federal frontier-AI regime under a new Commerce Under Secretary for AI Security. Large frontier developers would have to publish, follow and annually audit a frontier AI framework and publish a transparency report at each deployment. Very large ones would also retain a licensed independent verification organization. The Commerce Secretary could order a halt to development or deployment that presents an imminent catastrophic risk. The preemption clause covers the ground of state laws such as SB 53 and RAISE (frontier risk transparency, third-party auditing, incident reporting) but leaves deployment, child-safety and state-procurement rules to the states. It is a congressional route to the national standard EO 14365 calls for, with binding duties the EO does not create.

thresh
Frontier models trained with >10²⁶ FLOPs. Obligations scale with developer size: large (>$50M revenue and ≥$1B AI development spending over 36 months) and very large (>$5B and ≥$10B).
eval
Annual independent compliance audits for large frontier developers. Very large developers retain a licensed independent verification organization for ongoing assessment of their framework, risk monitoring and mitigations, including internal use.
timing
Transparency report before or at deployment of each new or substantially modified frontier model. Critical safety incidents reported within 72 hours (24 hours to law enforcement for imminent risk to life).
mit
Frontier AI frameworks must set risk thresholds, assess each model against them and decide on deployment and internal use; minimum framework requirements are set by regulation.
sec
Frameworks must cover cybersecurity for non-public model weights; weight exfiltration is a reportable critical safety incident.
halt
The Commerce Secretary may issue emergency orders suspending or restricting development, deployment or internal use of a frontier model that presents an imminent catastrophic risk.
acct
Audit reports go to the Under Secretary, the Attorney General and opted-in state attorneys general. Civil penalties up to $1M per violation, enforced by the Attorney General and opted-in state AGs.
update
Frameworks reviewed at least annually, with a justification published within 30 days of any material change; framework regulations reviewed yearly.
us-frontier-act ↔ ca-sb53new connection
Now

(absent)

Proposed

Would preempt state frontier-transparency, audit and incident-reporting duties such as SB 53's

us-frontier-act ↔ ny-raisenew connection
Now

(absent)

Proposed

us-frontier-act ↔ us-preemptnew connection
Now

(absent)

Proposed

Legislative route to the preemptive national standard EO 14365 calls for

Why it matters

This is the first bipartisan federal bill to impose frontier-specific safety duties: frameworks, audits, incident reporting, licensed verifiers and emergency halt orders. It would also preempt the state laws the map tracks (SB 53, RAISE). As a formally introduced bill it qualifies as 'proposed' under RUBRIC §1. It was introduced after the map's June snapshot.

Reasoning

Every element is taken from the introduced text on govinfo: sponsors and date, definitions (§2), framework, audit, transparency and incident duties (§4), licensed verifiers (§5), emergency orders (§8) and preemption (§9).

Uncertainty

Introduced only. The bulk data held no later version as of 2026-10-10, and committee status could not be checked because congress.gov refuses automated clients. Calling it 'a congressional route to the national standard EO 14365 calls for' is analysis, not a stated purpose of the bill.

Carried over, not re-verified

  • SB 53 and RAISE contain transparency, audit or incident-reporting duties (relies on the ca-sb53 and ny-raise entries, not re-checked here)

P-0107 v1 changeVerified externally

METR's nine elements are not the map's nine categories: say the categories are adapted

accepted v1 · 2026-10-10 · applied 2026-10-10 (2026-10-10-4.json)

Details, evidence and exact wording

Change

index.htmlpage text
Now

is a taxonomy of nine elements that frontier AI safety frameworks address: capability thresholds, model evaluations, capability elicitation, timing and frequency, weight security, deployment mitigations, conditions for halting, accountability, and updating policies. This map applies the taxonomy as an orthogonal filter

Proposed

identifies nine elements that frontier AI safety policies share: capability thresholds, model weight security, deployment mitigations, conditions for halting deployment, conditions for halting development, full capability elicitation during evaluations, timing and frequency of evaluations, accountability, and updating policies over time. This map adapts them into nine coverage categories — merging the two halting conditions and adding model evaluations as a category of its own — and applies them as an orthogonal filter

index.htmlpage text
Now

The orthogonal coverage analysis applies METR's nine elements (originally a taxonomy of corporate safety frameworks) to the full set of mechanisms.

Proposed

The orthogonal coverage analysis applies nine categories adapted from METR's common elements (originally a taxonomy of corporate safety frameworks) to the full set of mechanisms.

index.htmlpage text
Now

applied across METR's nine common elements of frontier AI safety policies.</p>

Proposed

applied across nine categories adapted from METR's common elements of frontier AI safety policies.</p>

Why it matters

The FAQ tells readers (and LLMs that ingest the JSON-LD) that METR's taxonomy consists of the map's nine categories. METR's own list differs: it has two halting elements and no separate 'model evaluations' element. Citing METR for a list it does not contain misattributes the map's own design choice.

Reasoning

METR's Dec 2025 page lists its nine components verbatim (metr-ce#thresh … #update): halting appears twice (deployment, development) and evaluations are discussed inside the other elements (metr-ce#eval) rather than listed. The map's categories therefore adapt METR's list. The edits keep the existing wording and add 'adapted'.

Uncertainty

Whether to rename categories is left alone; only the attribution changes. The cov-intro ('METR's framework taxonomy applied…'), the coverage header link text ('METR's 9 common elements') and build-llms.js ('METR's nine common elements as an orthogonal filter') use the same shorthand and are not changed here; the generated llms files follow build-llms.js.

P-0109 v1 changeVerified externally

Thresholds gap: no current lab framework tracks autonomous replication; revenue floors apply only to the US state laws

accepted v1 · 2026-10-10 · applied 2026-10-10 (2026-10-10-4.json)

Details, evidence and exact wording

Change

index.htmlpage text
Now

The labs set capability thresholds (CBRN, cyber, autonomous replication, AI R&D); the binding regulations set eligibility thresholds (10²⁵ or 10²⁶ FLOPs plus revenue floors).

Proposed

The labs set capability thresholds (CBRN, cyber, AI R&D, loss of control); the binding regulations set eligibility thresholds (10²⁵ or 10²⁶ FLOPs, plus a $500M revenue floor for the main US state duties).

Why it matters

The example list describes the lab frameworks of 2023–24. OpenAI moved autonomous replication to an untracked research category in v2, and the current Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta and xAI frameworks do not use it, while loss of control/misalignment now appears in most. 'Plus revenue floors' implies the EU AI Act has one; it does not.

Reasoning

Current domains: Anthropic RSP v3.4 rows (S-0006#5: chem/bio, misaligned AI in high-stakes settings, automated R&D); OpenAI v2 tracks bio/chem, cyber, AI self-improvement and lists Autonomous Replication and Adaptation among Research Categories (S-0095#2, S-0095#4); GDM v3.1 CBRN, cyber, harmful manipulation, ML R&D and misalignment (S-0102#3, S-0102#7); Meta v2 chem/bio, cyber, loss of control (S-0107#2); xAI CBRN, cyber, loss of control, harmful manipulation (S-0108#2). EU presumption is compute only (S-0002#10); the $500M floor is in SB 53 (S-0150#4) and RAISE (S-0033#9) for large frontier developers, while SB 53's 10²⁶ tier alone triggers transparency and incident duties (P-0057).

Uncertainty

Korea's decree adds capability and risk criteria to its 10²⁶ threshold (P-0102), still an eligibility test; not spelled out to keep the sentence short.

Carried over, not re-verified

  • No binding instrument yet sets the second kind (analytic; SB 53 §22757.12(a)(2) obliges developers to define their own thresholds but sets none)

P-0110 v1 changeVerified externally

Evaluations gap: the AI Act requires evaluation with adversarial testing, not third-party evaluation; the GPAI Code adds external evaluation

accepted v1 · 2026-10-10 · applied 2026-10-10 (2026-10-10-4.json)

Details, evidence and exact wording

Change

index.htmlpage text
Now

The EU AI Act requires it for systemic-risk GPAI.

Proposed

The EU AI Act requires model evaluations with adversarial testing for systemic-risk GPAI, but external testing only as appropriate; the GPAI Code goes further and calls for independent external evaluation.

Why it matters

'It' refers to mandatory third-party evaluation; Article 55 does not mandate third-party evaluation, so the sentence overstates the one binding example the gap gives.

Reasoning

Art. 55(1)(a) requires model evaluation including adversarial testing (S-0002#14); recital 114 says this happens 'as appropriate, through internal or independent external testing' (eu-aia#rec114); Annex XI asks systemic-risk providers to describe 'internal and/or external' adversarial testing. The GPAI Code (non-binding) requires independent external evaluations unless exceptions apply (S-0044#8).

Uncertainty

The AI Office could expect external testing in practice through the Code; the Act's text does not require it.

Carried over, not re-verified

  • Korea's Framework Act requires risk management plans
  • Everywhere else, evaluations happen because labs publish them, AISIs request them under voluntary access agreements, or independent evaluators (METR, Apollo) do them.

Timing gap: Illinois adds 72-hour incident reporting from 2027; the EU duty is GPAI serious-incident reporting, not AI Office post-market monitoring

accepted v1 · 2026-10-10 · applied 2026-10-10 (2026-10-10-4.json)

Details, evidence and exact wording

Change

index.htmlpage text
Now

California SB 53 (15 days), NY RAISE (72 hours), Korea (lifecycle reporting), and the EU AI Office\'s post-market monitoring are the binding instances. Outside those four, no statutory incident reporting for frontier models exists.

Proposed

California SB 53 (15 days), NY RAISE and Illinois (72 hours, from 2027), Korea (lifecycle reporting), and the EU AI Act\'s serious-incident reporting for systemic-risk GPAI are the binding instances. Outside these, no statutory incident reporting for frontier models exists.

Why it matters

'Outside those four' is no longer true: Illinois's Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act (signed Jul 2026) requires 72-hour critical-incident reports. And post-market monitoring under the AI Act is a high-risk-system duty overseen by market surveillance authorities; the GPAI instance is serious-incident reporting to the AI Office.

Reasoning

Illinois §15(c) 72-hour reporting (S-0170#9), Act effective 1 Jan 2027 (S-0170#13); RAISE 72 hours (S-0033#5); SB 53 15 days (S-0150#10); AI Act Art. 55(1)(c) serious-incident reporting to the AI Office (S-0002#15) versus Art. 72 post-market monitoring for high-risk providers (S-0002#18); Korea Art. 32 lifecycle risk management with results submitted to MSIT (S-0293#6, S-0293#7).

Uncertainty

Illinois appears on the map only if P-0066 is accepted; the fact stands either way.

Carried over, not re-verified

  • Pre-deployment timing is the easy part: the EU AI Act, China's GenAI Measures, Korea's Framework Act, and the lab frameworks all require it (China's security assessment applies only to services with public-opinion attributes, see P-0099)

Weight-security gap: SB 53 (and RAISE, Illinois) require frameworks to cover securing unreleased model weights

accepted v1 · 2026-10-10 · applied 2026-10-10 (2026-10-10-4.json)

Details, evidence and exact wording

Change

index.htmlpage text
Now

BIS export controls touch the adjacent question of who can access frontier-capable hardware. No US state, no UK statute, and no other binding instrument covers weight security directly.

Proposed

California SB 53 requires the published frameworks of large frontier developers to describe how they secure unreleased model weights, and NY RAISE (2027) and Illinois (2028) copy that duty, but none sets a security level. BIS export controls touch the adjacent question of who can access frontier-capable hardware. No UK statute and no other binding instrument covers weight security directly.

Why it matters

The text says no US state covers weight security. SB 53, in force since Jan 2026, makes 'cybersecurity practices to secure unreleased model weights' a required part of each large frontier developer's framework, which the developer must comply with; RAISE and Illinois use the same wording.

Reasoning

SB 53 §22757.12(a)(7) (sb53#a7) within the framework duty to write, implement and comply (S-0150#5); RAISE §1421(1)(g) (raise#g; effective 1 Jan 2027, S-0033#3); Illinois §10(a)(7) (il#a7; framework duty from 1 Jan 2028, S-0170#5). None prescribes a security level.

Uncertainty

Whether a 'describe your practices' duty counts as covering weight security 'directly' is a judgment; the statutes do make it a compliance obligation. The map's ca-sb53 and ny-raise entries carry no 'sec' coverage note; adding one is an entry decision not proposed here.

P-0114 v1 changeVerified externally

Halting gap: China can order services suspended; lab halting commitments have weakened (Anthropic, Meta)

accepted v1 · 2026-10-10 · applied 2026-10-10 (2026-10-10-4.json)

Details, evidence and exact wording

Change

index.htmlpage text
Now

The EU AI Office can order recall (Aug 2026 onwards). The GPAI Code calls for halting at systemic-risk thresholds. Seoul commitments asked labs to commit to it. Every lab framework includes it. That\'s essentially the whole list. No US state, no other national statute, no other multilateral instrument can compel a frontier developer to pause.

Proposed

The EU AI Office can order recall (Aug 2026 onwards). China\'s GenAI Measures let regulators order a non-compliant service suspended. The GPAI Code calls for halting at systemic-risk thresholds. Seoul commitments asked labs to commit to it. Every lab framework includes halting conditions, though several have weakened: Anthropic ties its delay commitments to what competitors do, and Meta\'s v2 replaced "stop" with "develop with mitigations". That\'s essentially the whole list. No US state, and no other frontier-specific statute or multilateral instrument, can compel a frontier developer to pause.

Why it matters

The map's own China entry says firms have had services suspended, and Art. 21 of the GenAI Measures provides for ordering suspension — a compelled pause the gap says does not exist. 'Every lab framework includes it' no longer conveys that Anthropic's RSP v3 made delays competitor-dependent and Meta's v2 dropped 'stop'.

Reasoning

S-0290#6 (Art. 21: ordered to suspend the relevant services); EU recall power S-0002#20, enforcement from 2 Aug 2026 S-0280#1; GPAI Code Measure 4.2 (S-0044#3); Seoul commitment IV (S-0034#8); RSP v3.4 Appendix A (S-0006#12); Meta v2 change log (S-0107#5); OpenAI v2 Critical halt (S-0095#6).

Uncertainty

General online-safety laws (UK Online Safety Act service-restriction orders, Australia's Online Safety Act) and Korea's Art. 40(3) order to stop a violation can also cut off a service; the rewrite scopes the closing sentence to frontier-specific instruments rather than list them. California's EO N-9-26 only asks for recommendations on a kill switch (S-0152#4).

Carried over, not re-verified

  • Conditions for halting are the rarest column in the matrix (internal count: 8 entries carry halt notes)

P-0116 v1 changeVerified externally

Default gap text: Illinois enacted mandatory third-party audits (2028) and incident reporting; the EU AI Act already requires GPAI incident reporting

accepted v1 · 2026-10-10 · applied 2026-10-10 (2026-10-10-4.json)

Details, evidence and exact wording

Change

index.htmlpage text (2×)
Now

Mandatory third-party auditing, compute KYC, statutory incident reporting beyond California and (from 2027) New York, liability rules for harmful outputs, and international verification regimes are proposed somewhere — binding nowhere yet.

Proposed

Compute KYC, liability rules for harmful outputs, and international verification regimes are proposed somewhere — binding nowhere yet. Mandatory third-party auditing of frontier developers is enacted only in Illinois (from 2028), and statutory incident reporting for frontier models only in the EU, California, and (from 2027) New York and Illinois.

Why it matters

This is the panel's default text. Two of its 'binding nowhere' items are now binding law: Illinois requires large frontier developers to retain a third party for an annual independent compliance audit (from 2028) and to report critical incidents within 72 hours (from 2027); and the EU AI Act has required serious-incident reporting from systemic-risk GPAI providers since Aug 2025, which the map's own gap:acct names.

Reasoning

Illinois Act §25(a) penalises failure to have a third party perform an independent audit under §10(d) (il#audit, S-0170#8), §15(c) 72-hour reports (S-0170#9), effective 1 Jan 2027 (S-0170#13); AI Act Art. 55(1)(c) (S-0002#15). No audit duty in SB 53 or RAISE (S-0150#17, S-0033#18).

Uncertainty

Liability, compute KYC and verification regimes were not re-verified (see carryover); the EU Product Liability Directive 2024/2853, which covers software, may bear on 'liability rules'. EU notified-body conformity assessment for some high-risk AI systems is third-party, hence 'of frontier developers'.

Carried over, not re-verified

  • Compute KYC, liability rules for harmful outputs, and international verification regimes are proposed somewhere — binding nowhere yet.

FAQ 'Which AI laws are binding with penalties?': update for Colorado and Texas (pow 4) and the Illinois Act

accepted v1 · 2026-10-11 · applied 2026-10-11 (2026-10-11.json)

Details, evidence and exact wording

Change

index.htmlpage text
Now

Five AI laws in this map are classed as binding with penalties: the EU AI Act (up to €35M or 7% of global revenue), China's GenAI Measures, Korea's AI Basic Act (~$21k per violation), California SB 53 (up to $1M per violation) and the NY RAISE Act ($1M/$3M). Most are phasing in; the two US state laws face a federal preemption push under EO 14365, which set up a DOJ task force to challenge state AI laws. The map's wider count of mechanisms that are binding with penalties also includes US BIS export controls and five regulators: the EU AI Office, UK Ofcom, the UK ICO, Australia's eSafety Commissioner and the Colorado Division of Insurance. The map classes the Colorado AI Act and Texas TRAIGA as hard law with weak enforcement, so they are not counted here.

Proposed

Eight AI laws in this map are classed as binding with penalties: the EU AI Act (up to €35M or 7% of global revenue), China's GenAI Measures, Korea's AI Basic Act (~$21k per violation), California SB 53 (up to $1M per violation), the NY RAISE Act ($1M/$3M), the Illinois AI Safety Measures Act ($1M/$3M), the Colorado ADMT Act and Texas TRAIGA (up to $200,000 per uncurable violation). Most are phasing in; the US state laws face a federal preemption push under EO 14365, which set up a DOJ task force to challenge state AI laws. The map's wider count of mechanisms that are binding with penalties also includes US BIS export controls and five regulators: the EU AI Office, UK Ofcom, the UK ICO, Australia's eSafety Commissioner and the Colorado Division of Insurance.

Why it matters

Your decisions changed the facts this answer summarises: Colorado and Texas are now classed as binding with penalties (P-0062, P-0063), Colorado's entry is renamed (P-0064), and the Illinois Act was added (P-0066). The answer still says five laws and that Colorado and Texas are excluded.

'the two US state laws' becomes 'the US state laws', since five are now listed.
